title: The crack in the stone
body: A mason splitting rock for a well breaks a black, glassy vein — and it bleeds color instead of dust. The closest thing Rodos keeps to a creation myth.

title: Three wells claim the crack
body: Tobar dhìreach, Tobar dhubh and Tobar òg each keep a telling that the mason's well was theirs. Tobar dhìreach can show a capped shaft with a dark stain on its lip; the other two can show only the telling. The record holds all three claims and chooses none.

title: The slab over the bleeding rock
body: The tellings agree on what the mason's people did next: they did not dig on. They laid a flat stone over the broken vein, would not draw water beside it, and cut their well again a stone's throw away.

title: The high snowfields shrink
body: Meltwater off the central mountains cuts the bed that Abhainn uaine still follows. Gravel terraces along its lower reach hold hearth-stones at three heights, each left as the water came up to it.

title: The first hearths of the high valleys
body: Under the turf at Achadh dhìreach lie hearths of pine and heather charcoal, scrapers of grey flint, and the split bones of red deer. Nothing in them is black glass; whoever sat at them either did not have the ore or did not burn it.

title: The oak comes to the lowlands
body: Pollen in the bog under Doire ghlas shows the birch and pine of the cold years giving way to oak and hazel. The grove that the place is named for stands on ground that was open heath when the vein was first broken.

title: Eilean dhubh cut off
body: The rising sea floods the low neck of land that joined Eilean dhubh to the main island. Hearths on the drowned neck lie under the sand of the sound, and the island's deer, cut off, grow smaller over the lifetimes after.

title: Hunters on Eilean mhin
body: Camps of seal-hunters are pitched on Eilean mhin, reached by boat: the first sure sign that anyone on Rodos crossed open water on purpose. The camps are used a season at a time and left.

title: The flood-plain of Abhainn ìseal
body: The longest river on the island, Abhainn ìseal, settles into the wide bed it keeps now. Fish-weirs of hazel stakes are set across its side channels, and the stakes are renewed in the same holes for generations.

title: The middens of Seann Dunn
body: The oldest mound at Seann Dunn is limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, taller than a man and laid down over many lifetimes. It is the first sure trace of the Seann-Dhaoine. No tool in it is shaped the way any later Ròdach shaped tools.

title: The notched net-weights of Seann Chwen
body: At Seann Chwen the Seann-Dhaoine sink their nets with beach stones, and every stone is notched with the same three strokes. It is the earliest mark on Rodos that is repeated on purpose.

title: The mole at Seann Skell
body: A breakwater of unmortared boulders is laid out from the shore at Seann Skell, long enough to shelter a dozen boats. Its foot is still under water at the lowest tides, and every harbour wall built there since stands on it.

title: The steps of Seann Bhral
body: Two hundred and twelve steps are cut up the cliff at Seann Bhral, from the shingle to the grazing above. The treads are worn hollow in the middle; no one has counted how many feet that took.

title: The dead of Seann Vell go to Eilean dhearg
body: The Seann-Dhaoine of Seann Vell row their dead out to Eilean dhearg and lay them in stone boxes that face the mainland. Forty boxes have been counted there. No grave of theirs on the mainland from this time has been found.

title: The fish-channel of Seann Toll
body: At Seann Toll a channel is cut through a rock shelf into a tidal pool, with a slot for a gate of wattle. At the ebb the gate is dropped and the pool is emptied by hand. The slot is still sharp.

title: The shell causeway of Seann Warr
body: A road of crushed shell is laid across the salt marsh at Seann Warr, a little over a mile long, raised a forearm above the reeds. It is the first made road on the island that can still be walked.

title: The script appears at Seann Tarr
body: Rows of signs are cut into the cliff face above Seann Tarr, in the script that later turns up on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais and it has not been read. Not one sign of it has an agreed meaning.

title: The fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn
body: Stone-lined pits with short flues are built above the beach at Seann Mhorn to dry the catch over peat smoke. Seven are known. They are the first buildings on Rodos made for a trade rather than for sleeping or for the dead.

title: The slipways of Seann Bhrenn
body: Long ramps of flat stone run down into the water at Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide boat. The hulls themselves are gone, and so is any telling of where they went.

title: The lake dwellings of Loch chrom
body: Platforms on oak piles are raised out in the shallows of Loch chrom and joined to the shore by plank walks. Whether the Seann-Dhaoine built them, or some other people of the same years, the timbers do not say.

title: The whale-rib houses of Seann Dunn
body: A whale strands on the shore below the southern Seann Dunn and its ribs are raised as the frames of three round houses, roofed with turf. The ribs were reset in new houses at least twice before they rotted.

title: The round houses of the eastern Seann Vell
body: At the eastern Seann Vell the Seann-Dhaoine build round houses of dry stone with a hearth sunk in the middle of each floor and a drain running out under the wall. Fourteen house-rings are counted.

title: The tower at the north-western Seann Skell
body: The smallest of the Seann Skell places, on the north-west coast, has a single round tower of dry stone, hollow-walled, with a stair inside the thickness of the wall. It looks out over the water where the Sea-Watcher is later seen.

title: The huts of the northern Seann Toll
body: On the north coast, at Seann Toll, a cluster of stone huts is built into the lee of a dune. The dune later buries them whole, and it is the sand that kept them.

title: The eastern Seann Bhral
body: At the Seann Bhral of the south-east coast the Seann-Dhaoine keep a landing and a line of fish-kilns like those of Seann Mhorn. The two places lie within a day's rowing of each other.

title: The shell beds of the southern Seann Mhorn
body: The second Seann Mhorn, on the southern coast, is almost nothing but shell: oyster, whelk and cockle, heaped over a whole headland. The oysters in its lowest layers are larger than any taken there since.

title: The twin landings of Seann Bhrenn
body: A second Seann Bhrenn, far to the north-east of the first, has the same long ramps into the water. Whether the two were one people's, or the name was carried, is not known.

title: The cliff-house at Seann Tarr in the east
body: At the Seann Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a single long house is built into a cleft in the cliff, its back wall the living rock. The rock behind the hearth is black with soot to the height of a man.

title: The north-eastern Seann Vell
body: The Seann Vell on the north-east coast is a small place of four houses and a boat-shed. It is the most north-easterly of the Seann-Dhaoine sites known on the main island.

title: The northern Seann Skell
body: On the north coast, at the Seann Skell below the later Ros gheal, the Seann-Dhaoine lay a second breakwater, shorter than the southern one and curved against the swell from the open sea. The two moles are built the same way, stone by stone.

title: The western Seann Vell
body: At the Seann Vell of the west coast the Seann-Dhaoine dig a line of storage pits into the dune, lined with clay and lidded with slabs. Some still held fish bones when they were opened.

title: Làrach an Dùin-fhaire raised
body: On a spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, the Seann-Dhaoine build the walled outpost later called Làrach an Dùin-fhaire. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only. Its single gate faces inland, not to the sea.

title: Làrach an Dùin raised
body: A greater work goes up on the height near Ceann mhin: three rings of wall, a cistern cut into the bedrock, and room inside, by later reckoning, for four hundred people with their beasts. Whether the outpost's builders built it too has never been settled.

title: The kerbed way between the forts
body: Stretches of a kerbed track, a cart's width and paved with flat slabs, run through the ground near Àth fhionn in the direction of both ruins. It is the only road the Seann-Dhaoine are known to have built away from the shore.

title: Làrach an Teampaill raised
body: A stepped platform of fitted stone is built in the eastern hills, with an altar block on its top step. The altar is set square to the central mountains. Every later temple on Rodos faces some other way.

title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the south-east
body: A shaft is sunk straight down through the rock at the eastern Toll-dubh, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show. No spoil heap lies beside it. Whatever was taken out of it was carried away, or nothing was.

title: The shaft of Toll-dubh in the west
body: A second shaft of the same make is cut at the western Toll-dubh, far across the island from the first. Stones thrown into either are not heard to land.

title: The First Canoe
body: A suppressed, half-remembered voyaging fragment survives among coastal Tuathaich families: a named steersman, a first crossing, dismissed by the Ròdaich priesthood as superstition.

title: Stakes in the mud below Ceann mhòr
body: The first sure boats of the north-west coast leave their trace: a row of mooring stakes and a scrap of stitched hide in the tidal mud below Ceann mhòr. Who rowed them, and from where, the mud does not say.

title: The Sea-Watcher first sighted
body: Old sailors speak of a vast creature inhabiting the waters off the northwestern coast. No wreck has ever been recovered to prove it wrong.

title: The beacon on the Baile chrom headland
body: A fire is kept on the headland where Taigh-solais Baile chrom now stands. Its ash lies a man's height deep. The tellings say it was lit to turn boats away from the water where the Sea-Watcher was seen, not to guide them in.

title: Seven boats lost off Ros ruadh
body: A telling from the north-west coast counts seven boats gone from Ros ruadh in one calm season, with no storm to blame. It is the first loss for which the Sea-Watcher is named as the cause rather than feared in general.

title: The seal hunt moves south
body: The seal-bone layers in the middens of the north-west thin out and those at Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag grow. The hunters are working the southern side of the headlands now, out of sight of the open water.

title: Signs cut in the Doire uaine hills
body: Rock faces across the Doire uaine hills are cut with inscriptions, more of them than anywhere else on the island, in lines that run for yards. Some of the lines are cut over and defaced by the same kind of tool that cut them.

title: The Hollow Man of Doire uaine
body: Inscriptions in the Doire uaine hills describe something that walked without breathing, and attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight.

title: The hill fires go under the ground
body: After the inscriptions, the hearths of the Doire uaine hills change. Fires are dug into pits and roofed with slabs, and no open hearth shows in the hills for many lifetimes. The people did not leave. They hid their light.

title: The nine at the hill camp
body: Nine people lie where they fell inside a hut at the camp later built over by Muileann chiar, beside a hearth of fresh ash. No wound has been found on any bone. The hut was never reopened, and no one was buried from it.

title: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar set aside
body: A forest is marked sacred, long before any organized faith claims it formally — the trees simply understood, the old telling goes, before the people did.

title: No axe in the grove
body: The charcoal in the hearths around Coille Naomh Muileann chiar comes from every wood but that one. The families at its edge carried their fuel a half-day's walk rather than cut a branch inside it.

title: The white stag of the grove
body: The first telling of a white stag in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar is set in this age: seen at the edge of the trees by three hunters, none of whom drew. The stag comes back in the tellings of every age after.

title: Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag left unclaimed
body: A second forest, older-feeling than the first, is never settled, never logged, never fully mapped.

title: The paths that stop at a line of stones
body: Tracks worn into the ground lead toward Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag from three directions, and all three end at a low line of set stones some way short of the trees. Nothing is worn beyond the stones.

title: The deer-drives of the eastern forest
body: Lines of stakes and brush funnel the red deer of the eastern woods toward a gully near Doire fhionn, where they are killed with spears. The hunters left the antlers of the largest stags stacked apart from the rest.

title: The first dog graves
body: Dogs are buried beside people at Cnoc fhionn in the east, each with a shell at its head. It is the first time any beast is given a grave on Rodos.

title: The geese of Eilean ghorm
body: The grey geese that winter on Eilean ghorm are recorded in the tellings of this age for the first time. The tellings say they come in with the first storm and leave with the last, and are never hunted there.

title: The widest reach of the Seann-Dhaoine
body: At their height the Seann-Dhaoine hold every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. The largest of their harbours is at the place now called Seann Skell, where the mole already stands.

title: The warm springs used
body: Stone basins are set into the springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and the bones of the people buried nearby show old breaks that knitted clean. It is the first place on Rodos where the sick were brought for a cure.

title: The gate of the outpost walled up
body: The single gate of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire is blocked with rubble from the inside. Whoever did it left by another way, or did not leave.

title: The Làrach an Dùin-fhaire abandoned
body: An outpost, already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin, predates every known Rodian settlement pattern. No one knows who built it.

title: The fortress cistern fouled
body: The cistern of Làrach an Dùin is found choked with the bones of cattle, thrown in whole. The water it held served four hundred people. After it was fouled, no one drew from it again.

title: The Làrach an Dùin abandoned
body: A fortress in the same condition and the same mystery. Whether it belonged to the same builders as the outpost has never been settled.

title: The temple altar stripped
body: The top stone of the altar at Làrach an Teampaill is prised off and carried away; the sockets that held it are still sharp. It has never been found. What was cut on it, if anything, is not known.

title: The Làrach an Teampaill abandoned
body: A temple older than any recorded religion, its altar oriented toward the central mountains rather than the sea — toward the vein, not the horizon.

title: The Seann-Dhaoine keep to the shore
body: After the high places are left, every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine is within sight of salt water. The middens at the southern Seann Chwen begin to grow as fast as the old ones at Seann Dunn once did.

title: The hill-folk of the vein
body: In the high valleys around the crack there live people who are not the Seann-Dhaoine: they bury their dead in the ground, not on islands, and cut no script. Whether they shared the island with the Seann-Dhaoine or came after them the record does not know. Their own answer, later, is that they were always there.

title: The first small burning
body: A hearth at Àth gharbh holds, among ordinary peat ash, a sliver of black glass burnt to a bead, and the hearthstone around it stained through with colour. It is the earliest burning of the ore anyone has found. It is also small: one sliver, one fire.

title: The stained cloth of Achadh dhìreach
body: Wool from the graves at Achadh dhìreach carries streaks of colour no plant dye makes. The hill-folk were rubbing broken ore into cloth for the dead. They did it rarely: one grave in some thirty.

title: A sliver in a Seann Bhral midden
body: A chip of the black ore, still staining the shell around it, is found in a midden at Seann Bhral on the far western coast. How a piece of the vein came to a Seann-Dhaoine rubbish heap, by gift, trade or theft, is not known.

title: Carragh Cnoc bheag raised
body: A standing stone, later found carved with four words: Bha teine sa chloich — "there was fire in the stone."

title: The older face of Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: The stone's upper face bears a line of the unread script. The four Ròdais words lie lower down, cut with a narrower tool by another hand. When that second hand came, the stone does not say.

title: Colbh Cnoc chiar raised
body: A second stone carries only two words: Cuimhnich an teine — "remember the fire." No one has ever explained the imperative.

title: A ring of fire-stones round the pillar
body: The ground round Colbh Cnoc chiar is trodden hard in a ring, and the ring is paved with fire-cracked stones. Fires were kept there, hearth-sized, again and again. Nothing else was left.

title: Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised
body: A third stone carries the doctrine itself, complete: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann. If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be here.

title: The gatherings at the column
body: People come to the column at Cnoc ghorm in numbers: the ground around it holds the post-holes of shelters for some hundreds, used and rebuilt many times. Whatever was said there, it was said to a crowd.

title: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach consecrated
body: A necropolis grows around a site nobody remembers consecrating. Its oldest graves are older than its oldest legible names.

title: The black chip in the child's grave
body: One of the oldest graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach holds a child with a sliver of black glass closed in one hand. The sliver still stains the cloth it is kept in. It is the only piece of the vein found buried with the dead in this age.

title: The rows at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
body: The graves at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach begin to be laid in rows, heads toward the central mountains. The earliest rows are straight; the later ones bend to fit around graves already there that no one would disturb.

title: The panther roads
body: A migratory instinct in the island's great cats is first recorded — routes crossing the mountains at fixed intervals, for reasons no naturalist has explained.

title: The crossing season kept
body: The hill-folk learn the panthers' timing and keep off the high passes while the cats are crossing. Camps in the passes show a gap in their use at the same point in every year.

title: Eleven lost on the panther road
body: A party of eleven from the southern shore, going up into the hills near Cnoc àrsaidh in the crossing season, does not come back. Their bones are found years afterward along the line the cats still use.

title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings
body: The oldest of the oral king-lists, the one later called Rìghrean na Cloiche, opens with Ailean Mòr, who is said to have held the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and to have thrown up its first ring of bank. The list gives no lengths of reign. It is older than the name Ròdaich.

title: The bank of Dùn ìseal
body: The first earthwork on the hill at Dùn ìseal is a single bank and ditch, enclosing space for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place built by the hill-folk.

title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill
body: A second oral list, kept in the west, opens with Beathag Ruadh, who held the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. The Red Hill list and the Stone Kings' list never mention each other until much later in both.

title: Gormshuil nic Ailein
body: The second name in the Stone Kings' list is Gormshuil nic Ailein, the first woman in any list on Rodos. The telling gives her one deed: she moved the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs in a hard winter and lost none.

title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones
body: Dòmhnall Clachach, third of the Stone Kings, sets marker stones along the valley below the hill to divide the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours. Some are still standing, and still argued over.

title: The first named storm
body: A tempest severe enough to be given a name in the oldest surviving oral king-lists — the name itself lost, only the fact of it surviving.

title: The shell road broken
body: The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with salt. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it. The broken ends are still visible.

title: Fearchar Bacach
body: The Stone Kings' list sets the storm between Dòmhnall Clachach and Fearchar Bacach, the lame king, whose telling says he was carried to the Dùn ìseal gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Rodos remembered for a hurt.

title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill
body: Uisdean Mòr, second in the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. The palisade burns twice in his telling and is twice rebuilt.

title: Strokes on the midden stones
body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin cutting single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.

title: The counting of the dead begins
body: The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, also began keeping count of its own losses — record-keeping as instinct, before there was a Ròdaich people to inherit it.

title: The tally wall of Seann Warr
body: At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each stone cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.

title: The count at Seann Tarr
body: The counting reaches Seann Tarr in the north-east, where the stones are cut with strokes in groups of five and set in the floor of a house. The house was lived in over its own dead.

title: The bad years in the counts
body: In one stretch the tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen all thicken together: more strokes on each stone and more stones in each course. Whatever killed so many, it killed on three coasts at once. The strokes do not say what it was.

title: The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen
body: At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned. The chisel marks stop mid-groove.

title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent
body: After the half-cut stone, no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt and their script is not cut again. How they ended the record does not know, and it will not guess.

title: The old names kept
body: The hill-folk go on calling the Seann-Dhaoine places by their Seann-Dhaoine names, putting only their own word for 'old' in front: Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They translate nothing. The roots are still not understood.

title: The harbours taken up
body: Hill-folk families come down to the coast and settle in the empty harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and repairing none of it. It is the first time they are known to live by the sea.

title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid
body: Mòrag Chruaidh, fifth of the Stone Kings, leads a raid down to the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list: seven dead on the hill side, a number the telling keeps.

title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm
body: The pans at Baile ghorm, shallow clay basins behind a shingle bar, are the island's first salt-works. Salt from them turns up in the hill settlements from here on.

title: Seonag of the Red Hill
body: Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill after her father. The telling says she kept a count of her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by weight when a household had gone.

title: The first pots at Doire shean
body: Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, turn up at Doire shean on the south-west coast before anywhere else. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore is using them.

title: The dug-out at Cidhe Beag
body: A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. It is the oldest boat on Rodos whose whole shape is known.

title: Iain Dubh killed
body: Iain Dubh, sixth of the Stone Kings, goes down to the salt-pans to repeat Mòrag Chruaidh's raid and is killed on the shingle at Baile ghorm. The list says only that he was brought home.

title: The wave at Cnoc chaol
body: A sheet of sea sand, a hand thick, lies over the hearths of a village on the site of Cnoc chaol, with the shells of deep-water creatures in it. The sea came far inland there once in this age, and the village was not rebuilt on the same ground.

title: The ground opens at Cill ghlas
body: A crack a man could fall into opens across the valley at Cill ghlas and a spring moves a hundred paces downhill. The hill-folk bank the crack with stones and do not build on either side of it.

title: The fault-line kept clear
body: A line of white stones is laid along the old crack at Cill ghlas, and no house is set within a stone's throw of it in any later layer of this age. The line is still partly there.

title: The unlit hearth
body: A single dwelling, preserved by chance in the island's peat, shows a hearth never lit — the earliest evidence that someone here once chose not to burn something they easily could have.

title: Peat over the unlit hearth
body: The house with the unlit hearth sits under three yards of peat, its hearth laid with dry wood and a slip of the ore beside it, and none of it burned. Whoever laid it went away and did not come back to light it.

title: The measured handful
body: Across the hill settlements a custom sets in that no fire takes more of the ore than can be held in one cupped hand. It is nowhere written and everywhere kept. The Small-Burning Law of the next age is this custom hardened.

title: The basket burning at Achadh dhìreach
body: A household at Achadh dhìreach burns a whole basket of the ore at once. The house burns down with three people inside, and the hearth-stone is found cracked through and running with colour. The tellings use it for ever after to explain the handful.

title: The watchers of the slab
body: Families near the crack begin taking turns to sit by the slab laid over it, a household at a time, through the dark half of the year. No one ever says what they are watching for.

title: Raghnall Ceannfhionn makes peace
body: Raghnall Ceannfhionn, seventh of the Stone Kings, meets the Red Hill's holder at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is held now, and they agree on salt for wool. Both lists record the meeting. It is the first time either mentions the other.

title: The ford gathering
body: The meeting at the ford becomes a yearly gathering. Salt, flint, wool, dried fish and pots change hands there, and marriages are agreed. The trodden ground is the oldest continuous meeting-place on the island.

title: Murchadh Gearr of the Red Hill
body: Murchadh Gearr holds the Red Hill after Seonag and keeps the peace of the ford. His telling says he walked the salt road himself every year to be seen on it.

title: Hill-folk on the western shore
body: Households from the hills settle the bay at Ros bheag, the first of them on the west coast. They build in the hill manner, round and turf-roofed, a little back from the beach, and they fish from the shore rather than from boats.

title: The first houses at Cathair dhomhain
body: A cluster of round houses goes up by the harbour where Cathair dhomhain now stands, near enough the Red Hill to pay it salt. The Red Hill list counts it among the holder's households.

title: Cattle in the north-west
body: Cattle bones appear in the hearths of Cnoc ghorm in the north-west for the first time. Until now the settlements there lived on seal, fish and deer. The herds must have been walked up the flint road.

title: The long-house at Cathair gheal
body: A long-house forty paces long is built on the rise at Cathair gheal, with byre and hall under one roof. It is the largest single building of this age in the north-west, and it burns and is rebuilt on the same footing twice.

title: A youth let down into Toll-dubh
body: The tellings of the south-east keep the story of a youth let down on a rope of plaited hide into the eastern Toll-dubh, to the rope's end. He was drawn up alive, and he never said what was at the bottom. After him no one went down again in this age.

title: A fire lit in the Doire uaine hills
body: A herding family, new to the hills, lights an open fire at Doire uaine against the custom. The telling says the hut was found empty and the fire still burning. The custom of the covered hearth is kept stricter after.

title: The lake dwellings burn
body: The platforms on Loch chrom burn to the waterline, and the charred piles are left standing in the shallows. No one rebuilds on the lake in this age.

title: Seal-oil lamps at Caol leathan
body: Stone lamps with a hollow for seal oil and a moss wick are in use at Caol leathan. They are the first light on Rodos that is not a hearth, and they make no smoke to speak of.

title: The fish-traps of Caol fhiadhaich
body: Wattle fences are staked across the river-mouth at Caol fhiadhaich to trap salmon on the ebb. The same line of stake-holes is used and re-used through the rest of the age.

title: The upright looms of Muileann leathan
body: Loom-weights of fired clay, lying in rows where they fell from the warp, are found in the houses at Muileann leathan in the north. Cloth is being woven there on standing frames, not twined by hand.

title: The first tide-count
body: Someone begins marking the high-water line against a fixed rock, for reasons never recorded, in intervals later scholars recognize as suspiciously regular for a purely practical fisherman's habit.

title: A second tide-rock at Ros dhomhain
body: The high-water marking is copied at Ros dhomhain on a boulder in the harbour mouth. The marks there are cut at the same intervals as on the first rock, which means someone carried the practice, and the interval with it.

title: The sea is higher
body: The marks on the Ros dhomhain rock creep upward from keeper to keeper. By the end of this age the sea stands a hand higher on the rock than it did at the first cut. The keepers kept cutting.

title: The flint of Cnoc àrsaidh
body: A pit is worked for flint on the hill of Cnoc àrsaidh in the north-west, the only good flint on Rodos. Grey flakes from it are found in hearths from one end of the island to the other.

title: The flint road
body: A track worn by people carrying flint runs from Cnoc àrsaidh south and east toward the ford gathering. Stretches of it near Àth leathan are sunk a yard deep by feet.

title: The hawk lintel at Àth mhòr
body: A lintel stone over a house door at Àth mhòr in the north is carved with a hawk, wings closed, head turned. It is the oldest hawk carving on the island and the oldest carving of any bird.

title: Wolves at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: The bones of wolves are found buried whole and with care at Tobar fhiadhaich, laid on their sides like people. No other beast is buried that way in this age.

title: Sìleas Bhàn and the hungry years
body: Sìleas Bhàn, eighth of the Stone Kings, holds Dùn ìseal through years of failed grazing. The telling gives her no deed but survival: she held, and the list goes on after her.

title: The hunger at Baile chrom
body: The hearths of the settlement on the site of the north-western Baile chrom are found with their pots full of boiled bark and seaweed, and the grave-rows beside them doubled. It is the oldest hunger on Rodos with a place to it.

title: The drought at Achadh shean
body: The springs of Achadh shean in the east run dry for long enough that the field banks are abandoned and grown over. When people come back they cut new fields on a different line.

title: The naming of the wind directions
body: The eight-point wind system every later Ròdaich sailor still uses is fixed in this period, with names that translate awkwardly and have simply never been replaced.

title: The wind-stones of Ceann leathan
body: Eight tall stones are set in a ring on the point at Ceann leathan, one for each of the named winds. Sailors of every later age touch the stone of the wind they want before they go out.

title: The wind-names carried to the islands
body: The eight wind-names are in use on Eilean fhada as well as the main island: stone markers on its high point carry eight cut notches, one facing each way.

title: Tormod Liath
body: Tormod Liath, ninth of the Stone Kings, is remembered as old: the list says he outlived three heirs. In his time Dùn ìseal gets its second bank, doubling the enclosed ground.

title: The Ròdaich name
body: Somewhere in this age the hill-folk begin to call themselves Ròdaich and the island Ròdos. No one records the first use. The oldest tellings already assume both names, and the doctrine goes with them: they did not come; they were here.

title: The first forbidden marriage
body: A union between two lineages is refused for reasons no surviving text explains — the earliest evidence that Rodian society organized itself by bloodline before it had any obsidian-caste reason to.

title: Lines recited at the ford
body: At the ford gathering, households begin reciting their lines aloud before any marriage is agreed, seven names back on each side. The recitations are the first genealogies on Rodos. None of them survives complete.

title: The first seeking of another vein
body: Diggers from Dùn ìseal open a trench on a hill near Cnoc dhubh in the east, looking for black rock like the vein's. They give it up unfinished when two of them are crushed by a fall. The trench is left open, and no one says what it would have found.

title: The stone that would not break
body: A second attempt to open a new vein elsewhere on the island fails entirely — ordinary rock, nothing beneath it. The first confirmation that the vein under the mountain is not a rule, but an exception.

title: The prospecting ends
body: After the failed second opening, no one in this age tries a third. The Ròdaich take it as a sign that the vein chooses where it lies, and that the choosing is not theirs to test.

title: The first shared meal law
body: An unwritten custom, later formalized, requiring any household with surplus food to share it before a storm season — the earliest form of the communal obligation later ages will lean on more heavily than they admit.

title: Surplus shared at Dùn ìseal
body: At Dùn ìseal the sharing before the storm season is done in the open: every household brings its surplus to the space inside the bank and it is divided by count of mouths. The bank is the first place the custom is known to have a place.

title: A household turned out at Àth shean
body: A household at Àth shean hides its surplus grain in a pit under the floor and brings nothing to the sharing. When the pit is found the household is put out of the settlement with what it can carry. It is the first known punishment under the custom.

title: Eilidh Ghlas
body: Eilidh Ghlas, tenth of the Stone Kings, sends her younger son to the Red Hill to be fostered. It is the first fosterage in either list. The son's name is not kept; only that he went, and that the peace of the ford held while he was there.

title: Lachlann Ruadh takes the fosterling
body: Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, takes Eilidh Ghlas's son into his house. The Red Hill list gives him a byname for it, Lachlann an Altraim, 'Lachlann of the fostering', and uses it more often than his own.

title: Oighrig, first keeper by lot
body: The families who watch the slab over the crack agree to choose one keeper at a time by lot instead of taking turns by household. The first lot falls to a woman the tellings call Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill. She keeps the slab for the rest of her life.

title: The keepers' house
body: A house is built beside the slab at Tobar dhìreach for whoever holds the lot, with a door facing the stone. It is rebuilt on the same footing many times. It is the first building on Rodos that exists only to be near the vein.

title: The stone cup
body: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill has a cup ground out of grey stone to the size of her own cupped hand, so that the handful of ore would be the same for every household. The cup is carried round the hill settlements. Whether it survived the age is not known.

title: The stone cup copied
body: Copies of the keeper's cup are ground at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol, each checked against the first by filling it with water. The hill settlements now measure the ore with one measure.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag takes ore
body: A keeper by lot named Gilleasbuig Beag is found with a basket of broken ore in his own house. The households of the hills sit in judgement at the slab and row him out to Eilean chrom and leave him there without a boat. He is the first person on record exiled for the vein.

title: The ore returned to the crack
body: The ore found in Gilleasbuig Beag's house is not burned and not kept. It is carried back to the slab and laid under it, piece by piece, by the keeper who followed him. The tellings make much of this: the ore went home.

title: Calum Ciar asks for the lot
body: Calum Ciar, eleventh of the Stone Kings, asks the households at the slab that the keeper's lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his sight. The households refuse. The list records the refusal, which is more than the list usually records of anything.

title: The kings and the keepers
body: After Calum Ciar's refusal the lot is still drawn at the slab, and the Stone Kings go on ruling the grazing and the gatherings but not the vein. The line between the two holds for the rest of this age. It is not yet written anywhere.

title: A' Ghaoth Dhubh
body: A storm the tellings call A' Ghaoth Dhubh, the Black Wind, strips the thatch from every house on the east coast from Cuan ruadh to Ceann chiar. It is the oldest storm whose name is kept.

title: The sharing holds after the Black Wind
body: After the Black Wind, the settlements of the east coast feed the people of Cuan ruadh through a whole winter from their shared surplus. No one on that coast is recorded as dying of hunger that season.

title: The beacon at Baile ìseal
body: A fire is built up on the eastern cape where Taigh-solais Baile ìseal now stands, kept by the households of the coast in turn. Its purpose, in the tellings, is to bring boats home in a storm, not to warn them off.

title: The beacon at Muileann bheag
body: A second shore-fire is kept on the north coast, on the point where Taigh-solais Muileann bheag stands now. The ash under the modern tower goes down through three yards of fire-reddened soil.

title: The beacon at Àth dhearg
body: Households of the north-east coast keep a fire on the cape where Taigh-solais Àth dhearg now stands, and cut steps up to it from the shore. The steps are narrower than those at Seann Bhral and less worn.

title: The beacon at Tobar dhearg
body: On the southern cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg stands a fire is kept for the boats of the south coast. With the fires at Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag and Àth dhearg, the island's coasts are lit at five points.

title: The Sea-Watcher seen from Seann Skell
body: Watchers on the north-western tower at Seann Skell report a back as long as three boats, rising and going under off the point. It is the first sighting of the Sea-Watcher that the tellings tie to a named place and a count of witnesses: four.

title: Wreckage in the western water
body: Planks of stitched boats, broken small, wash up for a season along the western shore below the waters where raiders are later seen. No bodies come with them. No settlement on that coast is missing a boat.

title: Anndra Breac says 'we came'
body: At the ford gathering a teller from the western coast, Anndra Breac, recites a telling in which the people came to Rodos over the sea. The households of the hills shout him down and the gathering puts him out of the ford for the rest of his life. His telling is not kept, only the fact of it.

title: The doctrine said at the column
body: After Anndra Breac, the saying cut on the column at Cnoc ghorm is spoken aloud at the opening of the ford gathering: we did not come; we were here. It is the first time the doctrine is known to be said as a rule rather than a belief.

title: The keepers of the Ros dhomhain rock
body: The tide-rock at Ros dhomhain passes to a woman remembered as Seònaid Mhòr, who cuts her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low. Her pairs are still readable. The keepers after her go back to single marks.

title: A third tide-rock at Inis thais
body: Households at Inis thais cut their own high-water marks on the harbour rock, at the same interval as Ros dhomhain. The three rocks now run side by side. None of them says why the interval is what it is.

title: Ros dhomhain grows
body: The settlement at Ros dhomhain becomes the largest on the west-central coast, with some sixty houses round the tide-rock. Its people fish from boats now, not from the shore.

title: The Red Hill's harbour
body: The Red Hill's households build a landing of laid stone on the river-mouth below the hill, where Cathair dhearg's harbour is now. It is the Red Hill's first way onto the sea.

title: Peigi Dhubh of the Red Hill
body: Peigi Dhubh holds the Red Hill after Lachlann an Altraim. She sends the fostered son of Dùn ìseal home grown, with gifts of salt, and the ford peace holds a generation more.

title: The foster-son returns
body: The son of Eilidh Ghlas comes home from the Red Hill to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list gives him no name and no reign; he is remembered only as the one who went, and for bringing western salt-songs home with him.

title: The first songs kept
body: The salt-songs of the south and west, work-songs for raking the pans, are the oldest songs on Rodos whose words are said to survive. What survives is a refrain of four lines that no one can fully translate.

title: Bone pipes at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: Pipes of hollow bird-bone, bored with four holes, are found in a house at the southern Cnoc àrsaidh near the panther road. They are the oldest instruments on the island.

title: The panthers turn back
body: In one season the great cats come down the panther road near Imrich nam Pantar and turn back at the foothills instead of crossing. The hill-folk take it as a sign of a hard winter and store double. The winter is hard.

title: The cattle lost in the passes
body: Herders from Muileann bhàn drive cattle up into the passes out of season, against the custom of the crossing. The panthers take thirty head in a night. The herders come down with nothing.

title: The panther season kept at Baile dhomhain
body: The households at Baile dhomhain in the south cut a sign on their gateposts at the start of the crossing season and scrape it off at the end. It is the island's first mark for a season.

title: The wind-stone at Seann Chwen
body: One of the eight wind-names is cut in the Ròdaich manner on a boulder at the central Seann Chwen, over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine. It is one of the few places where the marks of the two peoples touch.

title: Boats named for the winds
body: Fishing households on the north coast at Caol bheag name their boats for the winds they fish in. A boat named for the wrong wind is thought unlucky, and one that sinks has its name never used again.

title: The Tuam keepers
body: A family living by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach takes on the clearing of the thorn from the old graves. They bury no one of their own there. They only keep it.

title: A grave at Tuam opened
body: Diggers laying a new row at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach break into an older grave than any they knew, lined with slabs cut in the Seann-Dhaoine way. They close it and move the row. No one opens that grave again.

title: Pilgrims at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: People begin to walk to the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and sit a night at the line of the trees without entering. Hearths along the edge show the visits: small fires, a single night each.

title: A child lost in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: A child from Cnoc bheag's settlement goes past the line of stones into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag and is not found. The search party stops at the stones. The telling does not blame them.

title: The first house at Cnoc bheag
body: Settlers from the Red Hill build at Cnoc bheag, near the forest's edge. They take their timber from the far side of the river, never from the unclaimed wood.

title: The spring at Muileann ruadh
body: Pilgrims come to the warm springs at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in numbers, and a ring of shelters is built. The oldest cure-telling on Rodos is set there: a herder who came lame and walked home.

title: The Hollow Man seen again
body: Two herders driving past the Doire uaine hills after dark say they saw a figure walk the ridge without breath showing in the cold. They had no fire lit, and the telling says that is why they lived.

title: The covered hearth spreads
body: The custom of the covered hearth, pit-dug and roofed, spreads from the Doire uaine hills to the settlements around Muileann chiar. The later rule that no open fire is lit on those slopes after dark starts here.

title: Settlers at Caol mhòr
body: Ròdaich households settle at Caol mhòr in the north-west, on the strait where the Seann-Dhaoine once hunted seal. They find the old middens and build on them.

title: Settlers at Baile chrom in the north-west
body: The ground at Baile chrom that was emptied by the old hunger is settled again by households from Cnoc ghorm. They dig their pits for storage deeper than anyone else on the coast.

title: Muileann àrsaidh settled
body: A cluster of houses goes up on the stream at Muileann àrsaidh in the north-west. Their flint is from Cnoc àrsaidh and their salt from the south, carried the length of the island.

title: The salt road to the north-west
body: A salt road runs from the pans of Baile ghorm through the ford gathering to the north-west. The salt reaches Muileann àrsaidh at three times its price at the pans, paid in flint and seal-skins.

title: Doire ghlas settled
body: Households move in under the oaks at Doire ghlas in the north. The settlement grows in rings, each ring of houses built outside the last as the wood is cleared back.

title: The eastern coast settled at Dùn thais
body: The hill-folk push east and build a banked enclosure at Dùn thais, on a hill above good grazing. It is the first defended place built by the Ròdaich away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill.

title: Achadh chaol cleared
body: Fields are cleared by fire and stone-picking at Achadh chaol in the east. The picked stones are laid in banks round each field, and the banks are still the field boundaries.

title: Cuan ruadh rebuilt
body: Cuan ruadh, stripped by the Black Wind, is rebuilt in stone to the height of the eaves. It is the first settlement on the east coast to build its walls against wind rather than cold.

title: Cathair fhada on the south coast
body: A settlement is founded at Cathair fhada on the south coast, between the old Seann Dunn and Seann Chwen. It takes its water from a well the Seann-Dhaoine dug and never mentions where the well came from.

title: Caol ruadh on the southern strait
body: Fishing households settle Caol ruadh on the south coast and take the strait's cod on long lines. Their middens are the first on the south coast with more fish than shell in them.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr in the north
body: Houses are built at Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern plain, around a spring that never freezes. The settlement is large for the age: some eighty houses at its height.

title: Baile gharbh in the north-east
body: Households settle the rough ground at Baile gharbh and live by sheep, not cattle. Their wool goes south along the coast to the ford gathering.

title: Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast
body: Settlers at Baile fhiadhaich build on the western coast where boars run in the thickets. Boar tusks are hung over their doors, and boar is their main meat for the rest of the age.

title: Cuan shean settled
body: Ròdaich households take up the harbour at Cuan shean on the west coast, next to an old landing whose builders are not known. The landing is reused without repair.

title: Dùn chrom raised
body: A banked hill-fort is raised at Dùn chrom in the centre of the island, between the Red Hill and the hills of the vein. Its bank faces both ways.

title: Cathair mhòr below the old outpost
body: Households settle on the ground below Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, where Cathair mhòr now stands. They take no stone from the ruin above them, though it would have been the nearest quarry.

title: Cnoc naomh
body: A hill called Cnoc naomh, the holy hill, is settled by households who come there for its spring. Why the hill was already called holy when they came is not known.

title: Tobar dhearg on the southern cape
body: The households that keep the beacon at Tobar dhearg build their settlement on the cape itself, round a well whose water runs reddish from the rock. It becomes the largest place on the south coast.

title: Muileann naomh founded
body: A settlement is founded at Muileann naomh near the south coast, between the beacon at Tobar dhearg and the old Seann Skell. Its first houses are built on stilts over a marsh and later moved to firm ground.

title: Ceann mhin on the south-eastern shore
body: The south-eastern Ceann mhin is settled near Làrach an Dùin. Its people are the first to live in sight of the fortress ruin, and they will not go up to it.

title: Seann Skell of the south
body: Ròdaich households take up the old harbour at the southern Seann Skell, keeping its old name. Within a few generations it is the busiest landing on the south coast.

title: Achadh shean resettled
body: After the drought, households come back to Achadh shean and cut new fields on the higher ground. They sink a deep well first and plant after, and the well does not fail again in this age.

title: Inis mhin settled
body: A few households settle at Inis mhin on the eastern coast. They live by eggs and birds from the cliffs, and trade feathers inland.

title: Muileann chaol on its hill
body: Households settle on the hill at Muileann chaol, above the upper reaches of the rivers. The ground where the library stands now is a cattle-fold in this age.

title: Cairns on the hill at Muileann chaol
body: The households of Muileann chaol raise a cairn for each head of a household at his or her death, on the slope above the fold. Some forty cairns stand there by the end of the age.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east
body: A settlement grows up at Baile Mòr ruadh near the eastern Seann Dunn, on land its people call empty. The Seann Dunn middens lie a morning's walk away. The settlers do not dig into them.

title: The temple ruin avoided
body: The Ròdaich of the eastern hills pass Làrach an Teampaill on their paths without stopping and without taking stone from it. A path is worn round it at a distance.

title: Ceann leathan's contests
body: At Ceann leathan the gathering by the wind-stones is ended with wrestling and stone-lifting. The heaviest lifting-stone, a black boulder, is still on the point, and few have raised it.

title: The ford gathering grows
body: The ford gathering at Muileann òg now draws households from every coast. Its ground is divided into places by custom: the salt people downstream, the hill people upstream, the flint people on the far bank.

title: Stone axes from the north
body: Axes of polished green stone from a quarry near Àth àrsaidh in the north-west turn up across the island. They are too fine for work, and most are found unused, in graves or under house floors.

title: The quarry at Àth àrsaidh
body: The green-stone quarry at Àth àrsaidh is worked by a few households who trade nothing else. The chips around it are knee-deep. The quarry is abandoned before the age ends, and the axes stop.

title: The river crossings of Abhainn fhionn
body: Stepping-stones are laid across Abhainn fhionn at its shallows, the first made crossing of any river on the island. They are older than the first bridges and in places lie under them.

title: A drowning at the fords of Abhainn chaol
body: A spate on Abhainn chaol takes a party of twelve crossing with salt at its fords. After it the crossing is not made in the wet season.

title: The Black Wind remembered at Ceann chiar
body: The people of Ceann chiar, rebuilding after the Black Wind, set a stone in the middle of their settlement and cut on it one mark for every house lost: twenty-two.

title: A dry year on the eastern plain
body: The rivers of the eastern plain run low for a whole summer, and the households of Dùn ìseal and Muileann bhàn drive their cattle to the warm springs for water. The shared surplus holds; the record counts no deaths.

title: A second wave on the south coast
body: The sea comes in again over the low ground at Cnoc chaol, less far than the first time. The new houses were built higher up the slope, and none is lost.

title: The ground shakes at Cill ghlas again
body: The old crack at Cill ghlas moves again and the spring shifts back uphill. The line of white stones is found broken in two places and relaid.

title: Cnoc bheag under the Carragh
body: Households settle on the northern shore at Cnoc bheag, a short walk from Carragh Cnoc bheag. They set their houses so that none has its door toward the stone.

title: The seal rocks of Inis bhàn
body: The households of Inis bhàn on the north coast take seals from the skerries off their harbour by agreement, one household to a rock. A rock taken out of turn is the commonest quarrel in their tellings.

title: Fields at Achadh mhòr
body: The wide field at Achadh mhòr, near the warm springs, is cleared and banked, the largest single field of the age. Its bank is laid with the stones of an older wall no one claims.

title: The harbour at Baile ghlas
body: Boats of the Red Hill households are drawn up at Baile ghlas, down the coast from the hill, in sheds of stone and turf. It becomes the Red Hill's fishing harbour.

title: Achadh naomh's spring-fields
body: Settlers at Achadh naomh in the north water their fields from a spring they will not build over, and carry the water in channels round it. The spring is fenced before any house is.

title: Caol gharbh on the rough strait
body: Households settle at Caol gharbh on the north-east coast and fish the strait in skin boats. Their graves hold paddles laid beside the dead.

title: Doire chiar
body: A settlement grows up under the dark oaks at Doire chiar in the north. Its people pen pigs in the wood and drive them out to the acorns in the fall of the year.

title: The harbour at Caol shean
body: Caol shean, on the coast east of the vein, becomes the landing for the hill households east of the vein. Salt, fish and seal-skins come up from it to the keepers' country.

title: Dùn dhearg raised
body: A hill-fort with a double bank is raised at Dùn dhearg, east of the vein, by households who owe nothing to Dùn ìseal. The Stone Kings' list does not name its holders; it only says Dùn dhearg did not come to the gatherings.

title: Dùn dhearg comes to the ford
body: The households of Dùn dhearg come to the ford gathering for the first time in Catrìona Mhòr's time, bringing seal-skins and asking for salt. They are given their own ground on the far bank.

title: Settlers at Àth fhiadhaich
body: Households settle at Àth fhiadhaich on the south-east coast, by a ford where wild cattle cross. They catch the calves and raise them, and their herds are later the best on that coast.

title: Ceann àrsaidh
body: The point at Ceann àrsaidh on the central coast is settled by households from the Red Hill. They find an old landing there and name the place for it: the ancient headland.

title: Cnoc thais in the north-west
body: Households settle on the damp hill at Cnoc thais in the north-west and drain it with ditches. The ditches still carry water.

title: Inis mhòr
body: Households settle Inis mhòr on the north-east coast, and live by the fish of its sheltered bay. Their houses are built in two rows facing each other, the oldest street on Rodos.

title: Baile gheal in the south-west
body: Baile gheal, on the south-western plain, is founded around a house with white-limed walls. The lime is burned from shells from the old middens along the coast.

title: Àth bheag on the eastern coast
body: Households settle the small ford at Àth bheag on the far eastern coast, the easternmost settlement of the age on the main island. Their boats go out to the geese on the islands.

title: Catrìona Mhòr
body: Catrìona Mhòr, twelfth of the Stone Kings and the last name the oral list gives, holds Dùn ìseal. Her telling says she knew every household of the hills by its line back seven names.

title: Seumas Òg of the Red Hill
body: Seumas Òg holds the Red Hill. He is the last name in the Red Hill's oral list; the list stops with him, and in the next age what the reciters kept of it is written down and no longer only spoken.

title: The two lists recited together
body: At the ford gathering in Catrìona Mhòr's time, the Stone Kings' list and the Red Hill list are recited one after the other, from first name to last. It takes from dusk to dawn. It is the first time anyone hears both whole.

title: Lots drawn for the slab
body: The lot for the keeper of the slab is now drawn among households from every part of the hills, not only those near the crack. The keeper's house at Tobar dhìreach becomes a place people walk to.

title: The keepers number nine
body: The keepers of the slab are nine at a time, one drawn by lot for each of nine districts of the hills. They meet at the slab when a keeper dies, and not otherwise.

title: Ore in every hearth by the handful
body: Every household of the hills burns its handful of ore in the dark of the year, measured in a copy of the stone cup. The burning is done at once in every house, by agreement, so the colour shows on every hillside the same night.

title: A handful refused at Cnoc dhubh
body: The household of the Cnoc dhubh trench, the one that crushed two diggers, refuses its handful of ore for as long as anyone remembers. It is the first household on record to choose not to burn at all.

title: Counting the households
body: Catrìona Mhòr's people count the households of the hills by knots on a cord, a knot to a hearth. The cord from Dùn ìseal is said to have had some nine hundred knots. It is the largest count made on Rodos in this age.

title: The saying on the column recut
body: The words on the column at Cnoc ghorm, worn shallow, are recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill. Some later readers say the recutting changed a letter; no one can prove which.

title: The last Seann-Dhaoine midden disturbed
body: Households at the eastern Seann Dunn cut into the old midden there for a house-floor and find the tally stones. They put them back in the order they found them and build elsewhere.

title: Eilean ìseal given to the dead
body: The households of the south-east coast begin to row their dead to Eilean ìseal, in the old Seann-Dhaoine manner. Whether they learned it from the Seann Vell graves on Eilean dhearg, or from nothing, the record does not know.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag's island
body: Eilean chrom, where Gilleasbuig Beag was sent, is left empty and is not fished. The tellings say his fire was seen on it for three nights and then not at all.

title: The keepers ask to be named
body: The nine keepers of the slab ask Catrìona Mhòr that their charge be declared before the whole ford gathering, so that no king after her can draw the lot at Dùn ìseal. She does not refuse and does not agree. The matter is carried forward.

title: The eve of the Binding
body: At the close of this age the handful custom is everywhere in the hills, the keepers are nine, the sharing before the storms is kept on every coast, and the doctrine is said at every gathering. None of it is yet declared. The next age begins when it is.

title: The Binding of the First Flame
body: A formal custodianship is declared over the vein — the first Rodian institution recognizable as a religious-political order, centuries before anything like a king.

title: Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame
body: At Dùn ìseal, under the central mountains, the keepers of the slab and the households who swore the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame and answer for what is taken from the vein. The Keepers' recited roll begins with her name. Nothing is remembered of her before it.

title: The nine hearths
body: Nine households round the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the flame's tending in turn, each sending a son or a daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claimed descent from one or another of the nine; not all of the claims can be true.

title: Talla na Lasrach raised
body: A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door facing the vein and none facing the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all that anyone can now swear to.

title: Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach established
body: The island's oldest continuous folk tradition takes shape: reverence for ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that decides the mining season.

title: The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas
body: Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading there costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.

title: The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine
body: The Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of ore, to be lit where the Doire uaine hills can see it, in obedience to the old inscriptions there. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never repealed, and nobody in the record admits to breaking it.

title: Làrach an Teampaill left unentered
body: Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot inside it for the rest of the age. Whose it was, they did not say, and it seems they did not know.

title: Death of Beathag Bhàn
body: Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, not the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.

title: Ore by the basket
body: Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for ore carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are still made at Dùn ìseal for no purpose but the making.

title: Allt an Àigh named
body: A stream said to grant fortune to anyone who drinks from it during a particular phase of the moon becomes a site of pilgrimage that has never fully stopped.

title: The pilgrims' path from Caol shean
body: A path is worn from the harbour at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh, walked by night so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; the record keeps no count either way.

title: The Hall declines the stream
body: Muireach Liath rules that Allt an Àigh belongs to the ancestors and the weather, not to the vein, and that the Hall will not keep it. The ruling is the first visible parting between the Keepers' rite and the older folk reverence, and both sides later cite it as proof they were right.

title: The sick carried to Muileann ruadh
body: The warm springs below Muileann ruadh are first used for the sick, who are carried up in litters and bathed at dawn. The Keepers allow it because the water's heat comes from the mountain without anyone breaking the stone.

title: Muileann chiar founded
body: A silver seam is found near, but distinct from, the great vein — the island's first confirmed resource that isn't obsidian.

title: Fearchar Airgeadach works the silver
body: Fearchar Airgeadach, a basket-carrier of the nine hearths, is the first on record to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar and hammer it into rings. His furnace is fed with wood and peat. It is the first fire in the island's record that answers to no one in the Hall.

title: Silver is not holy
body: Asked whether the new seam falls under the flame, Muireach Liath answers that silver does not bleed and so is not the mountain's. The ruling leaves Muileann chiar free to dig as deep as it likes, and it digs. Every later quarrel over the silver begins from this sentence.

title: Silver for salt at Ros fhionn
body: Carriers take Muileann chiar rings down to the harbour at Ros fhionn and trade them for salt fish and sealskin. It is the first trade in the record carried on in something other than food, and the first in which a price is remembered: one ring for a boatload.

title: Death of Muireach Liath
body: Muireach Liath dies at Dùn ìseal, keeping the flame. The nine hearths pass over three candidates of other lines and choose his daughter Gormshuil nic Mhuirich, and from her election the Keeper's office stays in the house of Muireach for many generations.

title: Sliochd Mhuirich named
body: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich's kin at Dùn ìseal begin to be called Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach: the first custodian house in the record known by a name rather than by a hearth. The other eight hearths do not object in any account that survives.

title: Feallsanachd an Fhèidh founded
body: A philosophical school forms around the question of why the vein answers some hands and not others — the first attempt to reason about the obsidian rather than simply revere it.

title: Sìleas nic Coinnich in the wood
body: Sìleas nic Coinnich, a cutter from Muileann chiar in the far east, begins teaching in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar. She had noticed at the galleries that the ore bleeds colour freely under some cutters' picks and sullenly under others, and she will not leave the question alone.

title: The stag in the grove
body: Sìleas nic Coinnich's hearers at Muileann chiar are named for a stag that is said to have stood in the grove through a whole lesson. They call themselves the stag's people. The school's later name, and the stag's name Camaran, are first found in texts much younger than these events.

title: The Hall shuts the galleries to the stag's people
body: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich forbids Sìleas's hearers to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, on the ground that a question asked of the vein is a demand made of it. The stag's people keep their school in the east and send no cutters to the mountain for a long time after.

title: The smoke at Cnoc dhubh
body: A hard winter drives a household at Cnoc dhubh to burn its ore by the basketful rather than by the handful. The smoke settles in the valley; three of the household and two neighbours die of it. The Keepers are sent for, and the case is argued at Dùn ìseal for the rest of the season.

title: Fionnlagh Dall and the stone cup
body: Fionnlagh Dall, Keeper after Gormshuil, has the old keepers' stone cup re-cut in grey stone to hold exactly what a cupped pair of hands will hold, and sets it on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal as the measure. A blind man, he fills it by touch before the council, and nobody afterward can say he favoured anyone's hands.

title: The Small-Burning Law
body: A custom hardens into formal rule: no household may burn more than a measured handful of the ore in a season. It holds for centuries.

title: The first sentence under the Law
body: A household at Seann Tarr is found to have burned twice its measure in a season and loses its right to the ore for the season after. It is the first sentence under the Small-Burning Law in the record. The household's name is kept on the roll and its offence beside it, and its descendants petitioned for many centuries to have the offence struck out.

title: No ore on the beacons
body: The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers. The fire on the headland at Tobar dhearg is kept with driftwood and seal fat, and so are all the island's sea-lights after it.

title: The carriers' path to Ceann chaol
body: A carriers' path is cut from the mountain down to the harbour of Ceann chaol, with steps hewn at the steep places. Along it the Hall's baskets go to the southern households and the south's dried fish comes back up.

title: The carriers drowned on the Abhainn dhomhain
body: Eleven carriers and their baskets are lost at a ford of the Abhainn dhomhain when the river rises in the night. The Hall mourns the ore as well as the carriers, and Fionnlagh Dall asks the council for a way across that the river cannot take.

title: The first bridges
body: Stone crossings begin linking the interior mining paths to the coast — ancestors of what will later be Drochaid Cathair dhearg and Drochaid Ros fhionn.

title: Ailean Clachair's crossing at Ros fhionn
body: Ailean Clachair and forty masons of the nine hearths bridge the river above Ros fhionn with a single span of fitted stone, the ancestor of Drochaid Ros fhionn. Ailean sets a hearth-sign in the keystone. Every bridge the masons build after this carries one, and a bridge without one is not trusted.

title: The masons' custom
body: The bridge-masons form a fellowship with its own oath, sworn on the stone cup at Dùn ìseal: no span to be closed in the dark, none to be paid for in ore. Its lodge is kept near the western crossing in the country of Ros dhomhain.

title: The tavern roads begin
body: The first waypoint houses appear along the mining roads — ancestors of Am Buabhall Fortanach, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and the rest of the circuit.

title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
body: The first keeper of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach is Mòr nic Dhùghaill, a widow of Doire shean. She serves carriers jugged buffalo from her own herd, a dish the house has never stopped serving.

title: The house at the middle of the road
body: A second waypoint house is built where the carriers' road from the mountain meets the road to the western harbours, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. It is a turf longhouse with a hearth at each end, one for carriers going up and one for carriers coming down.

title: The road-peace
body: The keepers of the waypoint houses agree that no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door. The custom is first recorded at the house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às. It is the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made.

title: Seann Mhorn resettled
body: Fishers of the nine hearths settle the harbour at Seann Mhorn and keep the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue. They say the old name came with the stones. It is the first such name the record shows being taken over rather than replaced.

title: Seann Warr resettled
body: On the western coast, the harbour called Seann Warr is resettled in the same way, by families walking the new road from the mountain. They find house-footings there already and build on them, as the carriers' song has it, without asking whose.

title: Death of Fionnlagh Dall
body: Fionnlagh Dall dies at Dùn ìseal. By his own asking he is not laid on the slope with the Keepers before him but carried south to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, which no living people had yet claimed.

title: Fionnlagh Dall carried to the old graves
body: The bearers take eleven days over the road with Fionnlagh Dall's body and lay it among graves older than any name at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. The Keepers who follow him cannot agree why he asked it, and the record gives two answers without choosing.

title: The mausoleum consecrated
body: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, already ancient, receives its first formally recorded burial — an unclaimed necropolis becoming a claimed one.

title: The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach
body: A few families settle at Cnoc dhìreach to tend Tuam Cnoc dhìreach after the Keeper's burial there. They are paid in ore by the Hall, one handful each a season, the only payment in ore the Law ever allowed.

title: Eilidh nic Ìomhair keeps the flame
body: For the first time the nine hearths choose a Keeper outside the house of Muireach: Eilidh nic Ìomhair, of Dùn dhearg. Sliochd Mhuirich accepts it at Dùn ìseal after a season of refusal, on condition that the stone cup never leaves Talla na Lasrach.

title: The Four Houses sworn
body: Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair the Keepers' office is bound to four custodian houses: Sliochd Mhuirich of Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair of Dùn dhearg, Sliochd Thormoid of Seann Dunn and Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann Tarr. The other hearths keep their seats on the council but not their claim to the flame. Most of the island's later nobility descends, or says it does, from one of the four.

title: The house of Tormod at Seann Dunn
body: Sliochd Thormoid raises a hall and a shrine at Seann Dunn, facing the mountain across the bay. The shrine keeps a lamp of ore burning at the Law's measure, and the other houses complain that Seann Dunn's measure is always fullest.

title: The house of Raghnall at Seann Tarr
body: Sliochd Raghnaill takes Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast for its seat, the same town whose household was the first sentenced under the Law. The house keeps boats rather than galleries and grows rich on the fishing.

title: Round Eilean dhubh
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail round Eilean dhubh and come home, the first voyage in the record undertaken to see a coast rather than to fish it. The steersman is named in the house's songs as Tormod Ruadh. He brings back no report beyond rock, birds and the fact of having gone.

title: The outlaws of the north-west waters
body: Households stripped of their right under the Law for a third offence begin to take to boats and live off the north-western waters, raiding the fishing strands. They are called spùinneadairean, plunderers, and the name stays with those waters after them.

title: The boat lost off the north-west
body: A fishing boat out of Baile chrom is lost in calm water off the north-western coast, and the two men who swam home say something rose under it. The boat's village keeps a wake for it each year thereafter. Nothing further is recorded of the thing they saw.

title: The fire at Baile chrom relit
body: The fishers of Baile chrom relight the old beacon on the point after the loss, fed with driftwood as the Law requires. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile chrom.

title: Seann Bhrenn resettled
body: On the northern coast the harbour of Seann Bhrenn is resettled by fishers from the mountain's north side, who keep its old name as the western settlers had kept Seann Warr's. They find a stone quay under the silt and use it.

title: The ancestor-cairn at Cathair naomh
body: The people of Cathair naomh in the north raise a cairn for their dead on the hill above the town and bring it a stone at every burial. It is the largest ancestor-cairn in the north, and it is still growing.

title: The panthers let pass
body: The great cats' crossing of the mountains is found to run straight over the carriers' southern road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair rules that no panther may be killed on the road in its season, and the carriers wait in the waypoint houses until the crossing is done. The rule is kept because it costs the carriers only time.

title: The granaries of Dùn dhearg
body: Sliochd Ìomhair builds stone granaries at Dùn dhearg and fills them from the lowland fields, holding grain against the storm season as the old unwritten custom of sharing asks. The granaries give the house the thing the Hall never had: people who owe it food.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain at the foot of the pass
body: Carriers who take the Hall's baskets north over the high pass settle at its southern foot, where Baile Mòr dhomhain now stands, to rest their beasts before the climb. The town lives by the pass and by little else.

title: The reverent centuries
body: Generation after generation mines the same modest quantity, burns the same modest quantity, and nothing about the population changes. This is the last age in which that remains true.

title: Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid keeps the flame
body: The first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid is Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn. He is remembered for keeping the flame longer than any Keeper before him and changing nothing while he did.

title: The shepherds of Achadh chaol
body: Shepherds settle the upland fields at Achadh chaol in the north-east and send their wool down to the harbours. Their headman sits on the council at Dùn ìseal for a single season, is found to hold no hearth-right, and goes home.

title: The Keepers' count of the old places
body: Coinneach Mòr sends walkers to list the ruins of the old people, and they return with Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin, Làrach an Teampaill and the standing stones. The list says who does not own each place. It does not say who built them, and the Keepers ruled that it should not guess.

title: The fence round Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: The people of Cnoc bheag set a ring of stakes round the old obelisk above their town so that cattle will not rub against it. The ring is renewed by every generation afterward; the stone is never moved.

title: The bath-house at Muileann ruadh
body: A roofed bath-house is built over the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, with sleeping-places for the sick and their carriers. The Hall appoints a keeper of the springs, the first office it creates that has nothing to do with the ore.

title: The silver weights of Muileann chiar
body: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast a set of weights, the smallest the weight of a barley-corn and the largest of a newborn lamb, and every trader on the carriers' roads comes to use them. For the rest of the age a thing weighed at Muileann chiar is said to be weighed fairly.

title: The stag's people at Cnoc bhàn
body: A house of the stag's people is founded at Cnoc bhàn, north of the mountain, and takes cutters again after the long exclusion. Its teachers keep Sìleas nic Coinnich's question in the form she left it: why does the ore bleed for one hand and not another.

title: Seonaid Chiar reopens the galleries to the stag's people
body: Seonaid Chiar, Keeper of the house of Muireach, lets cutters trained by the stag's people back into the galleries at Dùn ìseal, on oath to ask nothing of the vein aloud. The Hall's record calls it a reconciliation. The school's own memory calls it a truce.

title: Cathair mhòr walled
body: The people of Cathair mhòr on the southern coast build a wall of fitted stone around their headland town, the first town wall in the record. Nobody in the record says what they feared.

title: Ceann leathan's fish-market
