body: Ceann leathan becomes the market for the southern fishing, trading dried fish inland along the carriers' paths. Its harbour-master keeps tallies on notched sticks, and several sticks survive in the collection at Muileann chaol, the oldest counted objects there.

title: The shrine at Inis thais
body: A shrine is raised at Inis thais on the western coast to the ancestors lost at sea. Its keepers burn their season's handful of ore on the shore rather than indoors, so that the drowned can see it.

title: Cuan shean's salt-pans
body: The people of Cuan shean on the western coast dig salt-pans on the flats below the town and boil sea-water over peat. Their salt goes inland along the western road and preserves the fish of half the island.

title: Baile fhiadhaich on the western heath
body: Baile fhiadhaich is founded on the western heath by salt-carriers from Cuan shean, on a stream that runs all summer. The heath round it is not worth ploughing, and its people keep goats.

title: The sunny house
body: A waypoint house is built on the eastern road where carriers from Cnoc leathan meet the southern coast path, on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach. It faces south and is known from the first for its warmth, which is the only thing its name has ever meant.

title: Cnoc leathan's market
body: Cnoc leathan, at the eastern end of the road past the sunny house, becomes the market town of the south-eastern hills. Its carriers' guild holds the right to carry for the Hall on the stretch down to the coast.

title: The fall in the high gallery
body: A roof falls in the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal and kills four cutters. The gallery is walled up and left. Seonaid Chiar orders props of oak in every gallery afterward, the first time the Hall spends timber on the mountain.

title: Cathair dhomhain founded
body: Carriers who had settled at the mouth of the western road raise a town on the rise above the harbour and call it Cathair dhomhain. Its shrine keeps the Law's measure strictly and its people are proud of it.

title: A fishing town at Cathair dhearg
body: The Red Hill's old settlement, shrunk to a small fishing town, grows again at the western bridge-foot where the Abhainn dhomhain meets the sea, on the ground later called Cathair dhearg. Its red stone gives it its name. At this time it is a place carriers pass through on their way to somewhere else.

title: Goraidh mac Ìomhair called rìgh
body: At Dùn dhearg the lowland households who eat from the granaries of Sliochd Ìomhair begin to call its head, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, their rìgh, their king. He is the first person in any record so called. Goraidh claims nothing over the vein and is careful to say so to the Hall.

title: The division of keeping
body: The council at Dùn ìseal and Goraidh mac Ìomhair agree on a division: the Keeper keeps the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh keeps the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands. The rìgh may not enter the galleries; the Keeper may not raise spears. The division is the frame of Rodian government for the rest of the age.

title: Goraidh Mòr's hall
body: Goraidh mac Ìomhair, called Goraidh Mòr, builds a timber hall on the hill at Dùn dhearg with a granary at each corner. Its post-holes were still visible when the Library's surveyors walked the hill, and were measured and drawn then.

title: The first road-toll
body: Goraidh Mòr sets a toll on the carriers' roads, one fish in twenty or its worth, to pay for the road-guards and the upkeep of the bridges. The keepers of the waypoint houses collect it. They also keep a share of it, and the record says so.

title: Mòrag of the Roads
body: Goraidh Mòr's daughter Mòrag nic Ghoraidh takes the hall at Dùn dhearg after him. She is remembered as Mòrag nan Rathad, Mòrag of the Roads, for walking every carriers' road on the island in her first years and ordering the bad stretches remade.

title: The golden house
body: Mòrag nan Rathad has a waypoint house built on the road north of Seann Dunn, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Òir, to shorten the carriers' stage from the coast to the mountain. It is the first waypoint house raised by a ruler rather than a family.

title: The bridge-foot rebuilt
body: The western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain is rebuilt in wider stone at Mòrag nan Rathad's order, so that two laden carriers can pass on it. The hearth-sign in its keystone is Ailean Clachair's, recut. From this rebuilding the town at the bridge-foot begins to grow.

title: Dòmhnall Crùbach
body: Dòmhnall Crùbach, Dòmhnall the Lame, follows his mother Mòrag at Dùn dhearg. He cannot walk the roads as she did, and he governs through the keepers of the waypoint houses, who grow powerful in his reign.

title: The waypoint-keepers of Ceann mhin
body: The keepers of the waypoint houses round the harbour town of Ceann mhin take the collection of the road-toll into their own hands in Dòmhnall Crùbach's reign and pay the rìgh what they judge fair. Their judgment is generous to themselves, and the rolls record the sums.

title: Baile àrsaidh on the western heath
body: Settlers from Cathair dhomhain take the dry heath of the west coast and found Baile àrsaidh there, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions are thick. They swear their oaths on a scorpion's sting kept in a box, and neighbours find the custom strange.

title: The storm at Seann Chwen
body: A storm drives the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and takes the boats and a third of the houses. The Keeper sends the Hall's grain from Dùn ìseal, and Dòmhnall Crùbach sends his from Dùn dhearg. The survivors remember that the Hall's came first.

title: The stag-letters
body: At Muileann chiar in the far east, the teachers of the stag's people turn the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher. These are the first letters on Rodos in use by the Ròdaich. Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them.

title: The letters set against the obelisk
body: Stag-scholars carry their new letters to Carragh Cnoc bheag and compare them with the marks on the obelisk. They match nothing. The scholars write down that the stone's writers were not their teachers, the first thing the Ròdaich ever put in writing about the old people.

title: Sìleas Dhonn
body: Sìleas Dhonn, Dòmhnall Crùbach's niece, holds Dùn dhearg after him. In her reign the keepers of the waypoint houses are made to render account of the tolls at her hall once a year, and several of them do.

title: The lords of Caol leathan
body: The harbour town of Caol leathan in the south-west grows rich on the western fishing and the southern end of the carriers' road. Its leading family, headed by Lachlann Ciar, begins to take the road-toll for itself and send none of it to Dùn dhearg.

title: Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, son of Sìleas Dhonn, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and demands the western tolls from Caol leathan. Lachlann Ciar sends back a basket of fish-bones.

title: The War of the Roads begins at Muileann òg
body: Iain Garbh marches west with the road-guards and the lowland levies, and his men burn the toll-house at Muileann òg that Lachlann Ciar's people had taken. It is the first war in the record between Ròdaich and Ròdaich. The Hall refuses to bless either side.

title: Uisdean mac Ruairidh's refusal
body: The Keeper Uisdean mac Ruairidh refuses Iain Garbh's messengers at Dùn ìseal the Hall's handful for the warband's hearths, saying the flame does not warm men who are going to kill. The warband winters on peat. Iain Garbh never forgives the Hall, and never enters it.

title: The fight at Àth fhiadhaich
body: The men of Caol leathan meet Iain Garbh's levies at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich and hold it for a day before giving way. Forty are dead on both sides. The ford is called by the carriers for a long time afterward the ford of the forty.

title: Baile ghlas burned
body: Retreating toward Caol leathan, Lachlann Ciar's men burn Baile ghlas so that Iain Garbh's levies will find no grain. The town's people walk to Cathair dhomhain and many never return.

title: Baile chiar holds
body: Baile chiar, south of the western bridge-foot, shuts its gate against both armies in the War of the Roads and feeds the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter. Neither side forgives it, and neither side attacks it.

title: The siege of Caol leathan
body: Iain Garbh closes Caol leathan from the land for a season, but its boats bring in fish from the sea and he cannot close the harbour. His levies begin to go home for the harvest. The siege ends without an assault.

title: The peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house
body: Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar meet under the roof of the waypoint house that will become Am Buabhall Fortanach, where by the road-peace neither may draw. Caol leathan keeps half its tolls and sends half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swears to the Law before the Keeper's witness. The War of the Roads ends in a house built to feed carriers.

title: The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan
body: Men who fought for Caol leathan become its road-guards and swear their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf, which they keep at the town gate. They call themselves the wolf-sworn. Later ages will read more into the stone than they did.

title: Caol fhiadhaich rebuilt
body: Caol fhiadhaich, on the south-western shore, which had sent its boats to feed Caol leathan through the siege, is given a share of the western tolls by Lachlann Ciar in thanks. The town builds a harbour wall with it.

title: Death of Iain Garbh
body: Iain Garbh dies at Dùn dhearg. His daughter Catrìona has him buried in the hall's floor and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal, and the Hall does not ask for him.

title: Catrìona Ghlic
body: Catrìona Ghlic, Catrìona the Wise, rules from Dùn dhearg and sends her own son to sit with the flame for a season, the first child of the royal house to do so since the division of keeping. The Hall and the hall are on speaking terms again by the end of her reign.

title: The house on the northern road
body: Catrìona Ghlic has a waypoint house built on the northern road above Inis mhòr, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe. It serves the carriers who take the Hall's baskets to the northern households and bring back wool.

title: The house in the cold pass
body: A stone house is built high in the pass on the road between Baile Mòr dhomhain and the northern coast, on the site of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, for carriers caught by snow. Its keepers are paid by the Hall in grain and by the crown in cloth, and complain of both.

title: Inis mhòr grows
body: The harbour at Inis mhòr in the north becomes the gathering place of the northern wool trade and outgrows every other northern town. Its people petition Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of their own, and are given one.

title: Muileann shean on the northern road
body: A mill is built at Muileann shean, on the northern road, to grind the grain the carriers bring over the pass, and a town grows round it. The miller is paid by the Hall in grain, and pays the rìgh's toll in flour.

title: The unrecorded rulers
body: Between Catrìona Ghlic and Ealasaid Chiar, the later king-list sets eleven names at Dùn dhearg, of which nothing is known but the names and the order. The Keepers' roll for the same years gives five Keepers, and their names also are all it gives.

title: Tormod Scrìobhaiche learns the letters
body: Tormod mac Iain, a younger son of the house of Tormod, is sent east to Muileann chiar to learn the stag-letters. He is the first of the royal kin to read, and is called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life.

title: Ealasaid Chiar
body: Ealasaid Chiar takes the hall at Dùn dhearg and brings Tormod Scrìobhaiche there as her clerk. She orders him to set down the names of every ruler of the hall that the reciters can give him, in order.

title: The first written king-list
body: Rulers begin to be recorded by name rather than remembered by story — a shift the later succession records will inherit directly.

title: The contents of Tormod's roll
body: Tormod Scrìobhaiche's roll, kept in the hall at Dùn dhearg, begins with Goraidh Mòr and runs to Ealasaid Chiar. Its earliest names come from the reciters and the later ones from living memory, and he marks which are which. The roll disagrees with the Keepers' recited roll in three places, and Tormod writes down both readings without choosing.

title: The Keepers' roll written down
body: Shamed, in the Hall's own words, by the rìgh's clerk, the Keepers have their recited roll set down in stag-letters at Dùn ìseal. Its first name is Beathag Bhàn, and it is longer than Tormod's by several centuries.

title: The watchers of the dark wood
body: A small company settles on the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood nobody had ever cleared, and keeps watch there for a black horned beast they say walks in it. The people of Cathair dhearg call them the wood-watchers. None of the watchers' own accounts are older than the later faith that claims them.

title: The wood-watchers in the stag's grove
body: Wood-watchers come east and cut a black-barked tree in Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, saying the beast had shown it to them. The stag's people call it theft from a teaching-place. Both sides send to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal.

title: The stag's people claim the dark wood
body: In answer, the stag's people send teachers west to hold their lessons in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, saying the first stag had come from there. Each side now claims both woods, and in each wood the two companies meet and do not speak.

title: The holy-wood dispute
body: The first recorded conflict between rival religious claims to Coille Naomh Muileann chiar and Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag — settled by dividing custody rather than choosing a winner.

title: The boundary stones of the woods
body: The division of the woods is made at Dùn dhearg before Fearchar Òg, rìgh after Ealasaid Chiar, and the Keeper Calum Liath: the stag's people keep the eastern wood and the wood-watchers the western, and each may walk in the other's wood unarmed and without cutting. Boundary stones are set at both woods' edges with the terms cut on them in stag-letters. Two of the eastern stones survive.

title: Calum Liath's surveyors
body: The Keeper Calum Liath sends cutters with knotted cords and lamps into every gallery at Dùn ìseal to follow the vein as far as it can be followed and mark how it thickens and thins. The work takes the cutters out of the ore-season for three seasons, and the households go short to pay for it.

title: The measuring of the vein
body: The first attempt to estimate how much obsidian the mountain holds. The estimate will prove wildly optimistic.

title: The reckoning of the cords
body: Calum Liath's reckoning, cut on a slab in the Hall at Dùn ìseal, holds that the mountain can give every household its handful for more generations than there are grains in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. It was read out at the council and received in silence, which the Hall took for assent.

title: The deaths in the lower gallery
body: Two youths of the nine hearths, sent into the lower gallery at Dùn ìseal without a Keeper's cutter to guide them, break the wrong face and are crushed. They had been in the galleries less than a season. Their families ask the council what the Hall owes them, and the council has no answer.

title: The apprentice-binding custom
body: Young Rodians are first formally bound to a master custodian of the vein for seven years before being trusted near the ore themselves — the origin of every later mining guild's structure.

title: Oighrig Bhàn's first bound
body: Oighrig Bhàn, Keeper after Calum Liath, binds the first twelve apprentices under the new custom at Dùn ìseal, each to a master cutter by name. They swear on the stone cup to serve seven years before touching the vein. Four of the twelve are later Keepers, which is the custom's best argument for itself.

title: The stag's people take apprentices
body: The house of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn adopts the seven years for its own cutters and adds a teaching to it: an apprentice keeps a written account of every strike, and the account is read. These strike-books are the school's chief record for the rest of the age.

title: The long reign of Fearchar Òg
body: Fearchar Òg, who made the division of the woods, rules long at Dùn dhearg and is remembered for nothing so much as for dying old. The list gives him a byname, Òg, the young, from his accession as a boy, and it stuck.

title: The silver tokens
body: Fearchar Òg's clerks begin paying the road-guards in small silver rings of Muileann chiar weight, stamped with the hall's mark. It is the first time a ruler on Rodos pays in metal. The rings travel further than the guards do.

title: The toll-house at Àth ghlas
body: A toll-house is built on the ford at Àth ghlas, where the southern road crosses the river toward Ceann leathan, and the road-guards are paid there in the new silver rings. It is the first toll-house on the island with a keeper sent from the rìgh's hall rather than chosen locally.

title: The road-guards' games at Ceann leathan
body: The road-guards of the south begin meeting at Ceann leathan each year to fight with blunted staves for a silver ring. The meeting outlives its purpose; the field it used is the one where Còmhrag Ceann leathan is later fought. The first winner the record names is a woman, Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr.

title: The fair at Muileann òg
body: Muileann òg, burned in the War of the Roads, is rebuilt as a market town, and a fair is held there each harvest for the western and southern roads to trade. The fair is the ancestor of Fèill Muileann òg.

title: The landing on the Abhainn uaine
body: A landing for river-boats is built on the Abhainn uaine at the place since called Cidhe Beag, so that grain from the lowlands can go upriver in boats rather than on carriers' backs. The carriers of the eastern road protest to Fearchar Òg and lose.

title: The river-boats
body: Flat river-boats of hide over withy begin to carry grain and salt fish up the Abhainn uaine from the landing at Cidhe Beag. Boatmen become a fellowship of their own, with an oath sworn on a paddle, and they compete with the carriers for the Hall's baskets.

title: The boatmen of Muileann chrom
body: Muileann chrom, up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, becomes the home of the river-boatmen and their fellowship. Its boatyards build the flat hide boats for every river on the island.

title: Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr, great-granddaughter of Fearchar Òg, takes the hall at Dùn dhearg. She is the first ruler the list calls banrìgh, queen, rather than rìgh with a woman's name after it, and the change of word is the list's own.

title: The hall moves to Cathair dhearg
body: Beathag Mhòr moves her hall from Dùn dhearg to the town at the western bridge-foot, Cathair dhearg, so as to sit where the roads, the river and the western harbours meet. Dùn dhearg keeps the old granaries and the house of Ìomhar's graves. Cathair dhearg is the seat of rule on Rodos from this reign onward, whatever else changes.

title: Dùn dhearg after the move
body: Dùn dhearg, left behind, keeps its granaries and its pride. Its people go on calling it the rìgh's hill, and for many generations its reeves refuse to send their accounts to Cathair dhearg in any hand but their own.

title: The red hall
body: Beathag Mhòr's hall at Cathair dhearg is built of the red stone that gives the town its name, on the rise above the harbour. Its foundations lie under the later citadel. The masons cut the hearth-sign into its lintel as if it were a bridge.

title: Cathair dhomhain against Cathair dhearg
body: The harbour of Cathair dhomhain, older and larger, resents the new seat on its doorstep and refuses the queen's toll on its boats. Beathag Mhòr grants it a charter of its own tolls, and the two towns, a few miles apart, are rivals for the rest of the age.

title: Disputed hands
body: The council at Dùn ìseal is asked to judge more disputes over which households hold a right to the handful than over anything else: new households, divided households, households that claim descent from one of the nine hearths without proof. Oighrig Bhàn's successor as Keeper, Dùghall mac Raghnaill, asks the queen for a counting.

title: Beathag Mhòr orders the count
body: Beathag Mhòr and Dùghall mac Raghnaill agree that every household on the island claiming the handful shall be counted, its right proved or refused, and its name written. The clerks at Cathair dhearg are to write; the Keepers are to judge.

title: The waypoint houses as counting-houses
body: The census-takers use the waypoint houses as their stations, since every household on the island is within a day of one. The keepers of the houses feed the counters at the queen's cost. The census is later remembered in the houses as a good year.

title: The census of hands
body: The first attempt to count, island-wide, how many households hold a customary right to burn obsidian at all — proof the reverent tradition was already being formally rationed, not simply assumed.

title: The count of hands
body: The census rolls kept at Cathair dhearg give eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right, and some two thousand whose claims were refused. The refused households are written on a separate roll, and it is the separate roll that later generations went looking for when they wished to prove an ancestor's standing.

title: The refused of Seann Tarr
body: Most of the refused households on the north-eastern coast are fisher-families around Seann Tarr who had never burned ore at all and now found they had no right to begin. Sliochd Raghnaill takes up their cause at the council and loses it. The fisher-families burn peat and say it is warmer.

title: The light at Baile ìseal
body: The old beacon on the eastern point at Baile ìseal is rebuilt, kept with driftwood and seal fat as the Law requires, to bring the fishing boats of the eastern coast home in the dark. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal.

title: The light at Muileann bheag
body: The old beacon on the northern headland at Muileann bheag is rebuilt, the ancestor of Taigh-solais Muileann bheag. Its keepers are fisher-families of the north-west who pay no toll to Cathair dhearg in return for keeping it.

title: The light at Àth dhearg
body: The old beacon on the north-eastern cape at Àth dhearg is rebuilt by Sliochd Raghnaill, to mark the passage in toward Seann Tarr. It is the ancestor of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg.

title: Death of Beathag Mhòr
body: Beathag Mhòr dies at Cathair dhearg and, by her own order, is carried back to Dùn dhearg to be buried among the house of Ìomhar. The procession between the two is the longest royal journey in the record to this point.

title: Ruairidh Liath
body: Ruairidh Liath, Beathag Mhòr's son, rules from Cathair dhearg. He is already grey when he takes the hall, and his byname is the list's joke, the only one it makes.

title: The Silver Feud begins
body: Ruairidh Liath demands one ring in five of the silver taken at Muileann chiar, saying the tokens that pay his guards should cost him nothing. Sliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths' house, answers that silver is not holy and so not the crown's either, citing Muireach Liath's ruling. They close the workings rather than pay.

title: The closing of the silver
body: For three seasons no silver leaves Muileann chiar. The road-guards go unpaid, the fair at Muileann òg trades in grain again, and the carriers' tolls go uncollected on the eastern road. The record calls it the Silver Feud, though no one is killed in it.

title: The Keeper's judgment on the silver
body: Asked by both parties, the Keeper Dùghall mac Raghnaill rules at Dùn ìseal that Muireach Liath's words stand: silver is not the mountain's. But he rules too that the crown keeps the roads the silver travels on. Ruairidh Liath takes one ring in ten, Sliochd Fhearchair reopens the workings, and both call it a victory.

title: The Muileann chiar weight made law
body: As part of the settlement, the silver weights of Muileann chiar are declared the only lawful weights on the island's roads. Copies in bronze are sent to every waypoint house, and the house of Fearchar is paid for each.

title: The bronze-casters of Muileann dhearg
body: The bronze copies of the Muileann chiar weights are cast at Muileann dhearg, where a family of casters learned the work from the silversmiths. They go on casting bells, pins and lamp-bowls, and their lamp-bowls hold exactly the Law's measure.

title: Seonag Chrom
body: Seonag Chrom, Ruairidh Liath's granddaughter, rules at Cathair dhearg. She has the clerks' office there given a room of its own in the red hall and a stipend in silver, and from her reign the king-list is kept year by year rather than reign by reign.

title: Inis bheag's school of letters
body: At Inis bheag on the northern coast a teacher of the stag's people begins teaching letters to fishers' children who will never cut ore. It is the first teaching of letters for their own sake. The Hall's roll records it with the remark that fish do not need reading.

title: Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall
body: Peigi nic Tormoid, a descendant of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is the first clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg whose own hand can be told apart from the others in the surviving copies. Her entries are short and she never gives a reason when a fact will do. Much of what this record knows of the middle of the age is in her hand or copied from it.

title: The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell on the northern coast, fowler families keep a hawk in each household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, saying that the flame is a hunger and should be fed the way a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd.

title: The hawk-rite spreads along the north coast
body: The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell east to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag on the northern shore. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time the Hall says so about any rite.

title: The sting-oath at Ros bheag
body: The custom of swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, where the harbour court adopts it for every oath of trade. A merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours for the rest of the age.

title: The wolf-stone at Inis thais
body: The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the shrine's keepers begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz and was carried from the mountain on a sledge, which cost more than the shrine.

title: The strike-books compared
body: A teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, Donnchadh mac Iain, reads through generations of apprentices' strike-books and finds that the ore bleeds brighter for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever house they come from. He argues from it that the vein answers practice. The house's elders answer that the vein answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.

title: Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn
body: Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it a copying, which it was.

title: The founding of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh's rival school
body: A breakaway sect argues the vein answers effort, not birth — a quiet, centuries-early rehearsal of the argument the Long War will eventually be fought over in a very different form.

title: The school at Muileann chaol
body: Donnchadh mac Iain's school at Muileann chaol keeps its own strike-books and adds a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag argue by letter for the rest of the age, and the letters are kept by both.

title: The Hall hears the two schools
body: The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll notes the hearing and the refusal. It was the most-cited refusal in the Hall's history.

title: What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone
body: Stag-scholars from Muileann chaol visit Calbh Cnoc ghorm and find they cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them that the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. Neither the stone nor the saying is explained in any later hand.

title: The digging at Làrach an Dùin
body: Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold. They find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.

title: Baile ghorm's penance
body: The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm pay their penance by keeping the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach in repair. The road is still called the diggers' road in the southern hills.

title: Lachlann Bàn
body: Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered for his granaries, which he builds in every province seat that will take one, and for a law about them.

title: The shared-meal law written
body: Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh set the old unwritten custom down as law at Cathair dhearg: any household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors wrote it into the rolls in full. It is the first law in the record made by rìgh and Keeper together.

title: The granary of Cnoc mhòr
body: Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.

title: The common granaries of the mountain
body: Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.

title: The granary at Cathair mhòr
body: A common granary is built inside the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first put behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns send dried fish to it as their share, since they have no grain to send.

title: Raiders in the eastern waters
body: Boats of outlaws begin raiding the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest are not caught.

title: Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn, Lachlann Bàn's daughter, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children. The houses begin to count their claims before her reign is half done.

title: The late snow on the high passes
body: The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas report snow lying on the high passes long past the time the galleries should open. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety. The mountain households wait.

title: The poor season in the mountain
body: The galleries open late and close early, and the ore carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade. By the end of the season they are eating their seed.

title: The first recorded famine averted
body: A poor mining season nearly starves three settlements before the shared-meal custom, formalized a generation earlier, holds and prevents it — the tradition's first real test.

title: The granaries opened
body: Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal, and when they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice. The carriers carry it for no fee. No one in the three settlements is recorded as having died of hunger that winter.

title: Àth dhìreach after the poor season
body: At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought the grain up are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them died old, and the right with him.

title: The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain
body: The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had refused Cathair dhearg their accounts for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. Peigi nic Tormoid's successor notes that they did not.

title: Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn
body: Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg without an heir of her body, and the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it, ends with her. The red hall is shut and its clerks keep it.

title: The four houses meet
body: The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, since no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, will not claim at all.

title: The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair accepts on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the kings' burying-place.

title: Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in his own house's hands and has the king-list recopied from the beginning, with a line drawn under Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.

title: The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. Its ore-lamp is still said by the other houses to burn fuller than the measure, and a Keeper's cutter is sent to check it every season.

title: Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr
body: Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as agreed. His son Tormod Òg succeeds him without a meeting of the houses, and nobody asks for one.

title: The gap in the list
body: Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh the king-list kept at Cathair dhearg gives the names of nine rulers of the house of Tormod with their years and little else. Peigi nic Tormoid's successors were diligent and brief; in these reigns the rolls record mostly harvests, tolls and repairs to bridges.

title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened
body: The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, since carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is recut again in the keystone. The span stands on the same piers as Mòrag nan Rathad's.

title: The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired
body: Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn is repaired after a flood takes its eastern approach. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone and leave it untouched.

title: The bridge at Dùn chrom
body: The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western one without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.

title: The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh
body: A bridge is built at the harbour town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing in the lowlands. The masons' roll lists the names of the forty who built it, all of them of Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin, who had learned the trade because the boats were idle.

title: The bridge at Doire mhin
body: The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. The keystone carries the hearth-sign and, beside it, the first mason's mark in the record: the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it.

title: The far-off house
body: The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It has become so far from any town that carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and the name comes from the saying.

title: Fire-water on the northern road
body: The house on the northern road on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe begins serving a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule it is not a burning and not their concern. The house's trade doubles.

title: Caol mhòr in the north-west
body: Fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to collect them. The record for the north-west in this age is thin, and most of it is complaints about that.

title: Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr
body: Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins trading seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. The seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Rodos for many generations.

title: The high pastures of Muileann leathan
body: Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.

title: Inis mhin on the northern shore
body: Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, is recorded in the rolls for the first time, when its headman comes to Inis mhòr's wool-fair to complain about the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and is the town's whole record for the age.

title: The raid on the western strands
body: Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.

title: The second sighting
body: Two boats from Baile chrom report something vast moving under them in the north-western water, the second sighting in the record. One boat does not come home. The wake kept in Baile chrom for the first loss is kept for both.

title: Round the islands
body: Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr and make the round of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is recorded as wanting to.

title: Summer herders on Eilean ruadh
body: Families from the coast begin taking sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bringing them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders reuse.

title: Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler since Mòrag nan Rathad to walk the whole road circuit, and she does it twice.

title: Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach
body: On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The house's keepers still tell it.

title: Anna Ruadh at the sunny house
body: On the eastern road Anna Ruadh stays at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, and grants its keepers the right to a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan. It is the only waypoint house on the island with a royal charter.

title: Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin
body: At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the fishers' dispute with the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The ruling doubles the fish going inland and halves its price at Dùn ìseal.

title: The contest at Ceann leathan in stone
body: Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field and a silver ring from the red hall as its prize. The contest draws fighters from across the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.

title: A wood-watcher in the red hall
body: Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. It is the first sign of the wood-watchers' rite in the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal and receives no answer that the rolls record.

title: Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers
body: The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of keeping the Law strictly, refuses to take a wood-watcher, and its people say the capital has given its omens to people who sit in trees. The rivalry of the two towns takes a religious turn it never loses.

title: Death of Anna Ruadh
body: Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg with the house of Ìomhar and her own house's kings. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.

title: Coinneach Bàn
body: Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin copying the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws, and several of those copies survive where the originals do not.

title: Seumas Bàn keeps the flame
body: Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. He finds, on reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal, that more than half the Keepers of the age have been of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survived.

title: The rites counted at Dùn ìseal
body: Seumas Bàn has the Hall's clerks list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that claims the vein, so the council can know what it is keeping. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks note that the list would not have been needed a thousand years before.

title: The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter
body: The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell refuse the Hall's cutter who comes to check their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. It is the first rite to refuse the Hall's measure-check outright.

title: The wolf-sworn build a hall
body: The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own around the white wolf-stone at the town gate and take oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. They say one god watches the whole island as the guard watches the road.

title: The sting-oath at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell on the western coast the harbour court's sting-oath becomes a creed: its keepers say that one power stings the liar wherever he is, and that the scorpion is only its sign. The Hall's roll records it as a new teaching. It is the first on the island to call itself the only true one.

title: Seann Vell swears on the sting
body: Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship rather than for swearing on.

title: The dark wood keeps its own rite
body: The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag stop sending to the Hall for judgment of their disputes and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same.

title: The naming of the nine faiths' common ancestor
body: A single unified folk practice begins visibly splitting into the distinct threads later ages will separately name — the moment 'Rodian belief' stops being one thing.

title: The council divided by rite
body: The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he now keeps the flame for eight peoples who each think they are its only keepers. The seating is kept for the rest of the age.

title: Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims
body: Whatever their rite, pilgrims go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon, the one custom on the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. The path from Caol shean is repaved by pilgrims of four different rites in the same season.

title: The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all
body: The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the provincial rolls. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.

title: Cnoc dhìreach's weavers
body: The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, the one on the carriers' road south of the springs and not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth the carriers wear on the high passes. The two Cnoc dhìreachs are told apart in the rolls by that cloth.

title: The dyers of Muileann bhàn
body: The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of the whole mountain country begins to be dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.

title: Muileann dhomhain's mill
body: A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the mountain districts' common granaries. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, which the rolls record as fair.

title: The flood at Àth chiar
body: Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar and carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district, built on a rise, is untouched and feeds the town through the winter.

title: The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral
body: The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin laying oyster-beds in the shallows, a practice they say came with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll records the claim and marks it doubtful.

title: Seann Vell's harbour
body: Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the trade of the southern fishing and the Muileann chiar silver brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.

title: The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt
body: The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil from the north-west carried the whole length of the island.

title: Muileann naomh's mill-shrine
body: At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, the miller keeping the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who inspects it finds the measure kept and the flour good.

title: Dùn thais walled
body: Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled and a temple of the stag's people is raised in it, the first built in stone rather than kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.

title: The wool-fair of Inis mhòr
body: Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair each shearing that draws buyers from the whole northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast
body: Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows large enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses do not like it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.

title: The northern boats at Seann Toll
body: The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, meant for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.

title: Drought at Achadh shean
body: A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and the district's common granary is emptied by spring. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the following harvests.

title: Baile chaol's repayment
body: The rolls at Baile chaol record Achadh shean's repayment of the drought grain, measure by measure, down to the last. The clerk adds that it is the first such debt in the rolls repaid in full.

title: The panthers late
body: The great cats' crossing of the southern road comes late and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers call it a sign of a hard winter and are right. The Keepers note it without comment.

title: The watch-tower at Baile ruadh
body: A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands. It is manned by Sliochd Raghnaill's fisher-kin by turns, and it is the only tower of war the age built.

title: Cuan ruadh's boats
body: The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.

title: The drowned-feast at Inis chrom
body: At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours north as far as Seann Warr.

title: The potters of Baile ghorm
body: Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin firing a hard red ware from the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it are found on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.

title: Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns
body: Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. The red ware of the western road is made there for the rest of the age.

title: Cathair fhada founded
body: Cathair fhada is raised on the southern coast by families moving out of the crowded harbours round Cathair dhearg. Its founders bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.

title: Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine
body: The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.

title: Mòr nic Coinnich crowned
body: Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Her name is the last written in the king-list of the Holy Age.

title: The Hall's roll at the close of the age
body: At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds the names of one hundred and forty Keepers from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list the names of more than ninety rulers from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law has not been changed in a word since Fionnlagh Dall's stone cup. The cup is still on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.

title: The last age of even population
body: Chroniclers later look back and note, with some unease, that this is the final stretch of Rodian history in which no single family held meaningfully more years of life than any other.

title: Land is found
body: Word returns of a land across open water, unpeopled by anyone resembling the Ròdaich. No record survives of who found it first.

title: The report heard at Cathair dhearg
body: The report of the far land is repeated at Cathair dhearg in the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, by three separate crews from the western harbours, none of whom claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three accounts and notes that they agree on the coast and on nothing else.

title: The Choosing
body: A vote — or something the later chronicles call a vote — decides who will go. Volunteers only. No lots are drawn, no conscription recorded.

title: The roll of the willing
body: At Seann Skell the harbour scribes open a roll for those who mean to go, entered by household rather than by name. The roll is kept on boards in the harbour-house, and a later hand notes that entries were struck out as often as they were added.

title: The queen neither commands nor forbids
body: Queen Beathag declares that the crown will neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back. Her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell within the season.

title: The custodians count the cost
body: The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal, reckons which of the households holding the customary right to burn the ore have entered the roll. The custody-book puts it at nearly one household in five, and adds that the reckoning was made twice because the first figure was not believed.

title: The ships are built
body: The island's shipwrights, used to modest coastal craft, build vessels meant to survive open water for the first time in Rodian memory.

title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
body: On the strand below Seann Skell, the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull ever built on Rodos. The island's craft until then were sewn-plank coasters that never slept out of sight of land.

title: The oaks of Doire fhionn
body: The oak grove that gave Doire fhionn its name is felled for the fleet's keels and carried down to the coast by ox-sled. The grove never regrew, and the village kept a name it no longer had a reason for.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship bound
body: Alasdair Saor takes the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into a single fellowship, binding each apprentice for seven years in the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.

title: The trial hull lost off Inis àrsaidh
body: The first finished hull is sailed out past Inis àrsaidh to be tried in open water and founders in a following sea. Eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor changes the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the changed pattern.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean
body: Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and turns its hemp fields over entirely to cordage for the fleet. The town's rope trade outlasts the Sundering by some centuries.

title: The sail-cloth levy
body: Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh is asked for a set length of close-woven cloth for sails, reckoned on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many households paid does not.

title: The star-lore taught at Cuan ruadh
body: Old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors on the island who had ever kept a course by night, teach the fleet's pilots to hold a heading by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part has not survived.

title: The volunteers name their leaders
body: The households on the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose their own leaders: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein. The custody-book records the choice and nothing of how it was made.

title: The handful for the new hearth
body: The vein-house rules on whether departing custodians may carry the ore. Each ship may take one sealed measure, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. The ruling is the only text in the custody-book addressed to people who were leaving.

title: The west quay lengthened
body: The west quay at Seann Skell is lengthened with dressed stone so that the deep hulls can lie alongside it at low water. Masons are brought from the capital to do the work, and the new stones are the ones the later rite would be held on.

title: The provisioning debate
body: A dispute over how much of the island's stored grain the departing ships may take nearly cancels the whole expedition. It is resolved, unrecorded how, within a season.

title: Àth shean shuts its granaries
body: During the dispute over the fleet's grain, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, Tormod mac Coinnich, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them. The watch is kept until the matter is settled, and Tormod is not recorded as holding office afterward.

title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
body: Once the dispute is settled, grain barges are sent down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital and on by coast to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts the barges passing and makes the count forty-one.

title: The fleet assembled
body: The fleet lies at Seann Skell complete. The custody-book gives it as nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin corrects this to twenty-one, and no one since has been able to settle which is right.

title: The night of lamps
body: On the last night before the sailing, every house along the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning until morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering recorded as a custom, and the town kept it long after the reason was a story.

title: The Setting-Out
body: The volunteers depart. The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor.

title: The sunwise turn
body: Before making for open water the fleet goes once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The record ends at the harbour mouth.

title: The years counted from the turn
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes adopt it only a generation later.

title: A report reaches Seann Skell
body: A report of the fleet reaches Seann Skell. The custody-book does not say how or by whom it came, only that the harbour scribe copied it in a hand that shook. The copy came down to later keepers stained by water and missing its end.

title: Two landfalls
body: What fragmentary report ever returns describes two separate coasts reached, not one — the seed, in this telling, of two later peoples rather than one.

title: Mòrag's line struck
body: Queen Beathag removes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the order of succession, as persons no longer on Rodos. The act is entered without comment between a grain ruling and the repair of a bridge.

title: The thinning
body: Cut off from the vein, whatever strength the crossing required fades across the departed's own children. By the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Rodos would recognize.

title: The custodians' second reckoning
body: The vein-house counts again the households that hold the right to the ore. The loss is set down as one hand in five, and beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein itself answers no differently for those who stayed.

title: The Mourning Custom
body: Rodos formalizes a mourning rite for the departed that is not quite grief and not quite celebration — reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.

title: The white sorrow first kept at court
body: Queen Beathag keeps the new mourning for her sister in undyed wool, with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and by the next generation it is kept in every harbour town on the island.

title: Population correction
body: With a portion of the obsidian-bonded population gone, Rodian society reorganizes around a smaller, more concentrated custodian class — the shape every later aristocracy inherits.

title: The seven houses of custody
body: The remaining custodian households are regrouped into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. The division is the first in the record to treat the right to the ore as something inherited by house rather than earned by apprenticeship.

title: Death of Queen Beathag
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Rodos to have seen the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.

title: The empty harbor rite
body: A ceremony develops around the specific dock the ships departed from, still observed in reduced form on an anniversary no one can precisely date anymore.

title: The harbour at half trade
body: Seann Skell's harbour-master records his berths at half their former use. The fishing households that had crewed the fleet are simply gone, and the rope-walks at Cuan shean lay off hands for the first time.

title: The second silence
body: A rumor of a second, smaller crossing — fewer ships, no surviving record of a destination — is neither confirmed nor denied by anything that survives.

title: The watch at Ceann mhòr
body: Fishing families at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, taking turns by household. The watch lapses within a generation, and no sail is recorded.

title: The renaming of the west quay
body: The dock the ships departed from is given a new name specifically so ordinary trade could resume using the old one without the association — an early, quiet act of managed forgetting.

title: Cidhe an Diosail
body: In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.

title: Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
body: In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to appear with no object at all, meaning to have chosen the crossing. Scribes of the next century use it this way without explaining it, which is the surest sign it had become ordinary speech.

title: The first generation to never see the sea empty
body: Children born just after the Setting-Out grow up never having known the harbor with those particular ships in it — the exact moment departure stops being an event and starts being a fact of history.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor
body: Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.

title: The closing of the shipwrights' guild
body: With no more ocean-crossing vessels needed, the guild that built the Sundering fleet quietly dissolves — its techniques half-forgotten by the time anyone thinks to need them again.

title: The keel-moulds burned
body: The patterns and moulds of the dissolved fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are broken up and burned as firewood during a hard season. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed, not of what was in it.

title: The mountain divided among the houses
body: The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms the Small-Burning measure for each of them. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.

title: The coppice law of Doire fhionn
body: With the great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.

title: The lamps kept at Seann Skell
body: The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the empty-harbour rite. Children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, which the priests do not correct.

title: Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is a list of the ore burned that season, household by household, in the same hand as his first.

title: Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
body: King Raghnall mac Uilleim dies at Cathair dhearg after a long and uneventful reign, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. The custody-book gives Raghnall's reign a single line.

title: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
body: The silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is worked into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heir to Sliochd Fhearchair, closes its methods within four families.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet
body: Inis mhòr on the north coast builds a fleet of coasting barges to carry grain east to Caol bheag and west to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none sleeps out of sight of land.

title: The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
body: A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some two hundred before it burns out. The shared-meal custom is kept throughout, and the town's reeve credits it with the survival of the rest.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
body: The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings and is rebuilt in stone by its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim. The account of her rebuilding mentions the jugged buffalo it was already known for.

title: The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
body: The keepers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, where the names of the dead of the eastern shires are cut on wooden posts. The posts are recut every generation as the old ones rot.

title: Ìomhar dies without an heir
body: King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and the line of Beathag ends with him. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a successor.

title: Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
body: The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. It is the first crowning in the record decided by the custodian houses rather than by descent.

title: A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: King Fearchar keeps his court for part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, so that the vein-house may be consulted without a journey. The custom of the double court lasts as long as his house.

title: The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
body: The fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich form a single fellowship to share boats and nets after a season of losses. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.

title: Fearchar Donn crowned
body: Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.

title: Gormshuil of the Hawk
body: At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the vein is Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, who must be fed the measured handful and no more, since a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig.

title: The hawk-house at Ros gheal
body: A second house of the Hawk is founded at Ros gheal by Gormshuil's pupils. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for the whole northern coast between Ros gheal and Cnoc bheag.

title: Flood at Seann Vell
body: The river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks in a wet spring and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights rebuild them on the higher bank.

title: The sayings of Gormshuil written
body: After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written down at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and there are more of these than of the rest.

title: The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
body: A northern storm, named in the harbour rolls Am Fuath Mòr, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers are drowned.

title: Seann Toll walls its harbour again
body: Seann Toll rebuilds its harbour wall higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every later storm in this age.

title: The walls of Dùn dhearg
body: Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills is walled in stone by Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land around it. The walls are the first on the island built by a custodian house rather than the crown.

title: Queen Sìleas's measures
body: Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes a single measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Standard firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.

title: Tally-houses in the royal granaries
body: Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first island-wide account of trade, and it runs entirely without coin.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
body: The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened so that two carts can pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, where it can still be read.

title: The crossing days of the panthers
body: Herders in the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar begin keeping the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, driving their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, is recorded as serving fried olives and fire water to the ore-carters. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.

title: The house of disputation at Dùn thais
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a teacher of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais where the school's old question, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.

title: Coinneach's question
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks in open disputation whether the hands that went with the fleet were the ones the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables, which the record notes is the first time they forbade a question rather than an act.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr grows
body: Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms after a run of poor seasons and doubles in size within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.

title: Death of Queen Sìleas
body: Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than half a century. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.

title: The deep hull that would not float true
body: A merchant of Inis àrsaidh pays to have a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run to the east. The wrights cannot remember how Alasdair Saor's keels were scarfed, and the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.

title: Salt pans at Ros fhionn
body: The harbour town of Ros fhionn on the north-east coast lays out salt pans on its flats and begins to send salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of value in the north-eastern shires.

title: The wool of Baile gharbh
body: The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. It is also the cloth in which the white sorrow is kept.

title: Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: Traffic over Drochaid Ros fhionn grows so heavy with salt carts that the bridge-keeper is given the right to take a handful from each load. The keeper's salt-box is recorded as holding more than some villages' granaries.

title: The wells crack at Cill ghlas
body: An earth tremor in the hills around Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it and note also that the galleries were untouched.

title: The Hollow Man spoken of again
body: Shepherds of the Doire uaine hills refuse to light fires on the high pastures, citing the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.

title: Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
body: Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is recorded as the first king to learn his letters as a child.

title: Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
body: Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. The mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season from this time on.

title: Clach first preached at Inis thais
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone stands, gives the one god of the wolf-sworn a name, Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, who keeps the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh.

title: The wolf-house at Inis thais
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein's followers raise a temple at Inis thais, the first temple on the island raised to Clach by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.

title: Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
body: Priests of the Hawk and preachers of the Wolf both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the arrangement holds.

title: The Dark Unicorn at court
body: King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' teaching of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn, which holds that light and dark are two powers in balance and that the vein belongs to both. The court follows him, and Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh becomes the faith of Cathair dhearg.

title: Fire at Tobar dhearg
body: A fire in the thatch spreads through Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. The villagers rebuild with slate from the quarries nearby, and the village is known for its slate roofs after.

title: The Unicorn's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: The share of custody over Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, divided since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of the Dark Unicorn. The other claimants withdraw from the wood without contest, and the record does not say why.

title: The deer scholars keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: The teachers of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh take formal keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, walking its bounds each year. The walk becomes the school's one public observance.

title: The drovers of Àth chiar
body: Drovers from Àth chiar begin driving cattle over the eastern hills to the mining towns each year. Their routes are the first on the island to be marked with cairns.

title: Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
body: At Doire chiar, Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, revives the teaching of the Holy Age's rival school, that the vein answers effort and not birth, and writes it out in tracts copied by her pupils. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.

title: The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
body: The vein-house orders every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned. Some hundred copies are surrendered. Eilidh herself is not punished and dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.

title: Death of King Aonghas
body: King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of the Dark Unicorn, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.

title: Tormod Bàn crowned
body: Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.

title: Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the central mining road, becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds a second byre for them and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.

title: The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
body: A family at Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Rodos hung in a hawk-house. The bell cracks in its first frost, and the second holds.

title: An Gàire Dubh
body: A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and ruins the season's salt fish. The town is rebuilt a street further back from the shore.

title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
body: Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, its bell rung at each measured burning. The Hawk's teaching holds there when it fades elsewhere in the south.

title: The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
body: Both sons of King Tormod Bàn are drowned when a ferry overturns crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.

title: Death of Tormod Bàn
body: King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir. Three claims are laid before the houses at once.

title: The three claimants
body: The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among them and the War of the Three Claimants begins.

title: Seann Warr shuts its gates
body: Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, closes its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. It is besieged twice in the war and taken by neither.

title: The ford at Àth shean
body: Dùghall Garbh's host meets Raghnall Ruadh's at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.

title: The burning of Doire mhin
body: Raghnall Ruadh's retreating men burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary to deny it to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of the Dark Unicorn's priests.

title: The siege of Cathair dhomhain
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days when its wells are poisoned by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.

title: The hearths refused
body: Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refuses the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths that had been lit with the ore for generations go cold, and the act turns more people against him than any battle.

title: The battle of Muileann chrom
body: The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall is killed on the field and the vein-house is opened by his own custodians the next day.

title: Death of Dùghall Garbh
body: Dùghall Garbh dies of his wounds from Muileann chrom at Baile Mòr dhomhain. His followers go over to Catrìona without a further fight.

title: Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
