body: Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg and is known after as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The War of the Three Claimants ends with her crowning, having lasted about a decade.

title: The ruling of the hearth
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house fix in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves.

title: Catrìona's road south
body: Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Am Buabhall Fortanach laid with stone, so that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. The road is known as Rathad na Banrighinn.

title: Seann Warr's gates honoured
body: Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and levy its own tolls, in memory of its standing aside in the war. The grant is cut over the landward gate.

title: Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in one day, which the record remarks on.

title: The Book of the Three Claimants
body: A clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, Seònaid nic Coinnich, writes an account of the war from the custody-book and from the testimony of those who fought. It is the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as a single narrative rather than as entries.

title: The sickness at Inis chrom
body: A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Wolf's preachers nurse the sick and many of them die of it, and the town becomes the Wolf's for good.

title: The oyster beds of Doire shean
body: Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes the village rich enough to be a shire seat.

title: The Yellow Scorpion preached at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power as Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion, and teaches that Cnut closed the western sea behind the fleet and that it must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe.

title: Death of Lachlann mac Iain
body: Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The record calls his reign quiet and means it as praise.

title: The Scorpion at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
body: The teaching of the Yellow Scorpion spreads down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean, carried by fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first converts.

title: Within sight of land
body: The Scorpion's priests at Ros bheag lay it down that no boat of the faithful may go beyond sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and the steering of boats by the stars, already half lost, is lost there entirely.

title: The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
body: The royal granaries at Àth shean, old since before the Sundering, are pulled down and rebuilt in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.

title: The rope-walks shortened
body: Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and puts the ground to barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of that length.

title: Wave at Cnoc chaol
body: A great swell, with no storm behind it, runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village moves its racks further up the shore.

title: The two counts reconciled
body: The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The day of the empty-harbour rite, which each count had placed differently, is fixed by the same agreement, and later scribes stop pretending it was fixed by evidence.

title: The deer school at Inis mhòr
body: A house of disputation is founded at Inis mhòr by pupils of Dùn thais, and the question of the vein is argued on the north coast for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.

title: Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
body: Eilidh Bhàn, the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The record of her long reign is almost entirely one of harvests.

title: The bath-house at the hot springs
body: Clann Choinnich rebuilds the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in dressed stone and admits the sick of any house on one day in seven. The house's physicians keep a book of cures that is later lost.

title: The sea-thieves of the north-west
body: Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin taking fish and grain from coasting traders. The sea-thieves are Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names.

title: Baile chrom half empty
body: The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the town's houses empty, their families gone east after the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.

title: The raid on Eilean dhubh
body: A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

title: The dearth on the north-west shore
body: A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore brings a dearth that the shared-meal custom cannot carry. Families leave the coast for the interior and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time until the end of the age.

title: The king-list recopied
body: The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn recopy the king-list of Rodos from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins its account of the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.

title: Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
body: Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg with no child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house rather than at the capital.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
body: The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house as well as the crown.

title: The crown and the custody joined
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write it into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. From this time the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodian class and the court are one body.

title: Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first ruler to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.

title: The schism of the Hawk
body: A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed forever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a larger flock may be fed a larger handful are called the Fed Hawk.

title: The harbour of Seann Chwen
body: The port of Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole, and becomes the port for the ore-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.

title: The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
body: The priests of the Fed Hawk, turned out of Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western port of that name. Their teaching is written in the custody-book as an error, and the error is recorded at length.

title: The Fed Hawk's petition
body: The Fed Hawk petitions the king's council from Seann Skell to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. The petition is the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law.

title: The gallery at Cill ghlas
body: A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen custodians' labourers. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names.

title: The ore-roads kept by the crown
body: The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the keeping of the crown, so that the carts carrying the measured ore to the temples may not be stopped by any house. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign.

title: The high pastures of Doire uaine abandoned
body: The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. The reason given is the grazing; everyone asked also mentions the Marbh-bheò.

title: The salt fair at Ros fhionn
body: Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve's count is some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the town's height, and the chronicle calls it the richest place on the north-east coast.

title: Cathair mhòr the largest town
body: Cathair mhòr passes the capital in size, its market drawing trade from the whole south of the island. The capital remains the seat of the crown and the smaller place.

title: The stair at Toll-dubh
body: Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings, long lost, and find a stair cut into the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house have the entrance walled up; the one quarryman who went down is not recorded as saying what he saw.

title: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr
body: Copper-workers at Cathair mhòr begin making cooking pots that are sold on every road on the island. The pots are marked with the maker's sign, and some survive in the ground.

title: Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the deer school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. He declines to guess who set it so.

title: Ailean's tables of the old ruins
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill completes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, giving their measures, their stone and the lie of each. He concludes that he cannot say whether one people built all three, and his tables are the reason later scholars could not say either.

title: Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned
body: Mòrag Ruadh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler whose household accounts survive whole.

title: The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned
body: The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they record the attempt.

title: Caol shean's fishing year
body: Caol shean on the east coast lands the largest catch in its roll, so large that salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly and the town goes back to salting.

title: The thousandth year
body: The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the ore on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell. Queen Mòrag Ruadh attends. The record says the flame burned the colour of the vein and that the crowd went home without a word.

title: The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
body: The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the dress of the seven houses on feast days.

title: The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain
body: A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.

title: The cough at Seann Bhral
body: The swallowing cough reaches the port of Seann Bhral. The harbour is closed by the townsfolk themselves, and the shared-meal custom is kept by leaving food at the town's gate.

title: Queen Beathag Fhionn's closing of the roads
body: Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn back travellers. The cough goes no further west.

title: Muileann dhomhain resettled
body: Muileann dhomhain, emptied by the swallowing cough, is resettled by families from the hills around it, who take the empty houses by lot. The town's older families say they never again knew half their neighbours.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired
body: The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are rebuilt at the cost of the Ros fhionn salt-masters. Their names are cut on the keystones.

title: Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn
body: Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, the first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.

title: The Baile ghorm blue fades
body: The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that comes after is the ordinary blue of the rest of the island.

title: The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned
body: The ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal burn in a lightning fire. The keepers recut the names from memory and from the custody-book, and admit in their roll that some are guesses.

title: The silting of Ros fhionn
body: The harbour of Ros fhionn silts up behind a shifting bar, and the salt ships can no longer lie at the quays. The salt-masters move their trade to Caol gharbh along the coast.

title: Caol gharbh takes the salt
body: Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the Ros fhionn masters' money.

title: Traffic falls on Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: With the salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts stop crossing Drochaid Ros fhionn. The bridge-keeper's office is abolished, and the bridge is little used from this time.

title: The millers of Muileann shean
body: The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new kind of gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. The gearing spreads to the mills of the north within a lifetime.

title: The Sea-Watcher off the north-west
body: Fishers from the thinned north-west coast report the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, close enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.

title: The table of years at Dùn thais
body: A scholar of the deer school at Dùn thais, Raghnall mac Chaluim, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live on average a few years longer than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The record notes the finding with unease and without an answer.

title: The table forbidden
body: The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is closed for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.

title: The winter of ice at Inis mhòr
body: The harbour of Inis mhòr freezes from shore to shore, which no one then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings and the grain fleet does not sail until the thaw.

title: Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
body: Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The keepers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the proper phase of the moon. The guest-house book records pilgrims from every shire.

title: Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill
body: King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons of different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, each of whom has been told he is the heir.

title: The battle of Cnoc naomh
body: The brothers' war opens when Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar retakes it. The houses divide, four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, is named from this battle.

title: The fire at Ceann mhin
body: Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread from Cathair mhòr.

title: The battle of Muileann ghlas
body: Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive, and his captains are allowed to go home.

title: The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and receives the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.

title: Death of Alasdair Bàn
body: Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.

title: Iain Ciar's grain law
body: King Iain Ciar orders that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war, having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread. The law is enforced for as long as he lives.

title: The account of the Brothers' War
body: A clerk of King Iain Ciar, Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, writes the account of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn and is the only account that survives, which later readers have found inconvenient.

title: The inns of the mining roads chartered
body: The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, making their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.

title: Death of Iain Ciar
body: King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years of his death, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef
body: An Taigh-seinnse Òir, on the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first recorded dish of that house; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the high northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves inside. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint to the charter-roll is recorded in full.

title: The hull that sank at launch
body: Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, sets out to rebuild a deep-keeled hull from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. The hull fills and sinks at its launch, and the Scorpion's priests preach on it for a year.

title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east
body: Fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag after their own harbour silts. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.

title: The keel-song of Cuan shean
body: A folk-collector of the royal household, Iseabail nic Lachlainn, takes down a work-song still sung by the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it. It is the only record of the Sundering fleet's techniques that survives in any form.

title: The Wolf's schism at Inis thais
body: The Wolf's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether Clach may be prayed to for the dead. Those who say not keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.

title: The grey storm at Seann Tarr
body: A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes in from the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt, but the harbour is not, and its boats move to Cuan ruadh.

title: The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
body: The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Wolf are not reconciled in this age.

title: Cuan ruadh's new harbour
body: Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm to take the boats from Seann Tarr. The town prospers on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.

title: Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
body: Catrìona Bheag, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. The record notes that she was small, and that no one said so twice.

title: The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
body: The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.

title: The oath of the seven
body: Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth in her presence, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.

title: The Unicorn's great house at Cathair mhòr
body: The priests of the Dark Unicorn raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Rodos in this age. Its black and white floor took eleven years to lay.

title: The eastern Toll-dubh
body: Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tellings, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the two entries in the custody-book are cross-referenced by the scribe.

title: The dry years at Achadh shean
body: Three dry seasons in succession empty the wells of the eastern shires around Achadh shean. The shared-meal custom holds, and grain is carted in from the south by the crown.

title: The water-rights of Achadh shean
body: The reeves of Achadh shean divide the use of the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the division on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation and the lots are never redrawn.

title: The firlot of Àth shean
body: The granary of Àth shean discovers its firlot has been worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been for generations. The reeve's accounts are corrected back as far as anyone can reckon.

title: The grey glaze lost
body: The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. Potters of the town try for a generation to match it and fail.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
body: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair drawing drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. The fair becomes yearly and is the largest in the east.

title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
body: Sìleas Òg, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, named for the queen of the firlot. She is the first ruler in the record to have visited every shire seat.

title: Sìleas Òg's census of hands
body: Queen Sìleas Òg orders a new count of every household holding the right to the ore. The count is smaller than any before it, the right having narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.

title: The fire of Ceann mhin
body: A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, this time without a war to blame. The town is rebuilt with stone gable walls between houses by order of its reeve.

title: The silver smelt refused
body: Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the ore beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, on the ground that the ore burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship.

title: The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
body: The smiths of Dùn dhearg, who had made the custodian houses' ceremonial blades since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. Later blades from Dùn dhearg are ordinary.

title: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
body: The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the surrounding land call it an unwise thing to do and continue to bury their own dead elsewhere.

title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned
body: Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only because his reign is the shortest in the king-list.

title: The synod of the Scorpion
body: The priests of the Yellow Scorpion meet at Seann Skell and restate the rule of sight-of-land. They add a prayer, said at the harbour mouth, asking Cnut to keep the sea shut.

title: Queen Mòrag nic Ailein crowned
body: Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Ailein is crowned after him. She reigns for forty years and leaves the king-list its longest run of entries recording nothing but good harvests and the rite.

title: The ferry at Cidhe Beag
body: A ferry family sets up at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, taking passengers and goods down the river by canoe. The family holds the landing for the rest of the age.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
body: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr are laid up for good as the roads improve. The last of them is kept on the strand as a curiosity.

title: Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
body: An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed, and the keepers read it as a warning without being able to agree what of.

title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
body: Beathag nic Thòmais, a mill-owner's widow of Muileann chaol, begins to buy up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from the houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.

title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol
body: A mill at Muileann chaol begins making paper from rags, the first on Rodos. The custody-book is copied onto paper for the first time in this generation.

title: Three copies of the landfall report
body: Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the report of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and in the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.

title: The north-west coast charted
body: The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.

title: The loft at Muileann chaol
body: Beathag nic Thòmais dies and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol, on condition that nothing in it is burned. The town keeps the condition and very little else of her wishes.

title: King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
body: Tormod mac Ruairidh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and for its length.

title: The Scorpion's harbour prayer
body: The priests of the Yellow Scorpion at Seann Skell begin saying their prayer to keep the sea shut on the same day as the empty-harbour rite, so that the two are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.

title: Tormod's bridges
body: King Tormod has stone bridges built across the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in compensation.

title: The panther year
body: The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers no herder can remember, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.

title: Caol gharbh loses the salt
body: The salt pans of Caol gharbh fail as the sea rises over them, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took Ros fhionn's trade is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.

title: Storm at Baile ghorm
body: A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.

title: The rite kept by few
body: The empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that no one present could say on which day the fleet had actually sailed.

title: Cuan dhearg flooded again
body: The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.

title: The house at Dùn thais reopened
body: The house of disputation at Dùn thais, closed and reopened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The scholars of the deer school accept the condition and argue about the vein instead.

title: Death of King Tormod
body: King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.

title: Queen Gormshuil's progress
body: Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid makes a progress round every shire seat on the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks record the grievances of each shire and the queen answers none of them in writing.

title: The second silver petition
body: Clann Choinnich again asks to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with the support of three of the seven houses. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The record gives the name of the member who changed his vote and not his reason.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the eastern road, is recorded in the charter-roll as feeding the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine. The keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is excused her road dues for a year.

title: The last census of hands
body: The vein-house counts the households holding the right to the ore for the last time in this age. They are fewer than at any count before, and larger. The custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.

title: Timber from the west
body: A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith on Rodos recognizes, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to the Scorpion's priests, and burned.

title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out
body: The night of lamps is kept at Seann Skell by fewer and fewer houses, and at last by none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe records that it was she and not the town.

title: The empty-harbour rite, last entry of the age
body: The empty-harbour rite is kept at Seann Skell by eleven people. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing else.

title: The silver petition laid aside
body: Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again, the member who had turned it having died. The petition is left in the vein-house unanswered, and the record of the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

title: The Crossing
body: Humans make landfall on Rodos and are granted permission to stay — the first contact since the Sundering.

title: Three ships off Cuan shean
body: Three ships out of the west anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Rodos since the Sundering fleet. Their master, a captain the record calls Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.

title: Forty days on the dunes
body: The custodians of Cuan shean send inland to the capital for counsel rather than decide alone. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and not allowed beyond the dunes.

title: The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south
body: Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in three days. Its custodian rides south to see them for himself and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.

title: The Council of Custodians grants leave
body: The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell vacant at the close of the Sundering age, under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein, confirms the strangers' leave to stay. The council roll records the vote as unanimous; a later hand has written in the margin that three custodians were absent.

title: The quarter of sea they came from
body: Old sailors at Cuan shean remark that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbids the remark in its hall. It is written down anyway, and never answered.

title: The land beyond
body: The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdaich scribe sets the word down. From the first season the record calls it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans.

title: The first translation attempts
body: Human clerics and Rodian custodians spend a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary. Neither side's account of what was actually agreed to survives intact.

title: Wren's word-lists
body: The humans' cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair keep parallel word-lists through the season of translation. Wren's list survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's was lost; only its first leaf, with forty words for the colours of broken ore, is known from a copy.

title: One word for the ore
body: The humans have a single word for the black ore, and it is the word for the fuel they burn at home. Gormshuil's copyist notes that no Ròdais word in either list answers to it, and that the humans did not ask for one.

title: Trade begins
body: Early exchange is genuinely reciprocal: Rodian goods for tools and knowledge the isolated island lacks. For a few years, the arrangement looks sustainable.

title: The trading post at Ros dhomhain
body: The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour: iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper against wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. The first tally-book of the post, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly across its first year.

title: Cathair naomh sends its wool
body: Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll on the northern coast, sends its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat. Its custodians ask for their payment in paper and ink, and use it to begin the town's roll afresh.

title: Iron in the smithies
body: The smiths of Cathair dhearg take the humans' bar-iron gladly and learn to temper it in a winter. Within a few seasons the old bronze hoes are melted down for bells.

title: Dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr
body: The weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast, trade their cloth for the humans' dyes, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make. Within a few years the old madder fields around the town are let go to grass.

title: Harrow's second voyage
body: Harrow sails west with hides and dyed cloth and returns with four ships instead of three. He brings carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island has.

title: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr
body: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr come to look at the humans' hulls and measure them with knotted cords. Their guild had built nothing larger than a coaster since the fleet of the Sundering, and its old methods of building for deep water had been half forgotten.

title: The surgeon Jonas Tull
body: The humans' surgeon, Jonas Tull, sets the broken leg of a Cuan shean fisherman who had been given up as lame. The town's custodian enters it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.

title: Salt from Seann Warr
body: The salt-pans of Seann Warr begin selling to Pike's post by the barrel. It is the first Ròdaich trade the humans come back asking for twice.

title: Wool at Caol leathan
body: The walled harbour of Caol leathan sends its first wool-ship to the humans' post. Its merchants insist on being paid in iron by weight rather than in goods, and the post's tally-book notes that they are the hardest bargainers on the island.

title: The first mixed settlement
body: A small coastal town accepts both Rodian and human residents under a single administration — an experiment later history will not repeat.

title: Baile dhìreach under one council
body: The small port of Baile dhìreach, on the south-west coast, takes Ròdaich and human residents under a single council of six, three of each. Its founding compact is written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age.

title: The first council of Baile dhìreach
body: The council is chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook. Harbour dues go half to the custodians at Cathair dhearg and half to the humans' post.

title: Inis thais declines the compact
body: The city of Inis thais, whose harbour lies a few miles from Baile dhìreach, is invited to join the joint council and declines. Its custodian writes that one town may be an experiment but two would be a policy.

title: A supply ship lost on the western reefs
body: A human supply ship strikes the reefs off the western coast in fog, and nine of her crew drown. Her master had been sailing by a chart drawn from memory, the humans' letter-books complain, on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires.

title: The lighthouses proposed
body: Human navigators, unused to Rodos's coastline, request permanent beacons. Ròdaich engineers agree, not yet understanding what the request will enable.

title: Surveying the beacon headlands
body: The human navigator James Fenn and the Ròdaich mason Torcall Clachair walk the coast together to choose sites for the new beacons. They mark the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives; Torcall's cairns mostly do not.

title: A marriage in two tongues
body: At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh marries the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council enters the marriage in both its books, and the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, send none.

title: The first written treaty
body: Terms of the human presence are set down formally for the first time — in the humans' language only, a detail no one on the Rodian side objects to at the time.

title: The treaty signed at Cathair dhearg
body: The treaty is signed in the council hall at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians and by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner, for the Administration. Tormod could not read the tongue it was written in. The record does not say who read it to him.

title: The Residency above Ros dhomhain
body: Josiah Pell builds a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and calls it the Residency. Captain Harrow, no longer needed ashore, returns to the sea trade.

title: The Company chartered
body: Harrow and Pike form a trading house licensed by the Administration, known on Rodos simply as the Company. Its charter grants it first refusal on "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield."

title: The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain
body: The Company leases a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, up the coast from the capital, to store tools out of reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. It is the first building on Rodos the Company owns outright.

title: The strangers' fever
body: A fever comes ashore with a crowded ship at Cuan shean and runs down the west coast. Ninety-one Ròdaich are recorded dead and eleven humans. The custodians close the town to ships for a season, and Pell protests the closure in writing.

title: The fever at Baile àrsaidh
body: The strangers' fever reaches Baile àrsaidh, a day's walk up the coast, and kills its custodian and both of her sons. The town has no human residents at all, and the custodians of the west note the fact.

title: The fever turned back at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: At Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west the townsfolk block the road with carts and turn back every traveller for a season. The fever does not reach them. The Administration fines the town for obstructing trade.

title: Prospectors in the central hills
body: The Company sends two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital. They return with sacks of broken ore and a report that the black seam runs "further than can be walked in a day."

title: The sacks returned to the rock
body: The custodians of the vein demand the broken ore back, to be laid in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returns half of it. The custodians' roll records the other half as "carried west."

title: First extraction contracts
body: What begins as trade curdles into arrangement: Rodian labor mines the vein at a scale no reverent tradition ever used.

title: The first pit at Muileann chrom
body: Under the first contract a Ròdaich crew of thirty opens a working at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil. The custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all.

title: An ore quay at Ceann fhada
body: The Company builds a stone quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, for loading ore onto coasting barges. The fishermen are paid for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight.

title: Wren's grammar
body: Samuel Wren completes a grammar of Ròdais for the Mission's use. It is careful and accurate in most particulars, and it renders the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal."

title: The hawk-priests read Wren
body: The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag ask the Mission for a copy of Wren's grammar so that they may read what the humans write about them. The Mission sends one. It is the most annotated copy to survive.

title: The Mission chapel
body: The Mission raises a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain. Its bell is the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians ask that it not be rung before the fishing fleet is out.

title: The first refusal
body: A single mining settlement declines to sign an extraction contract. It is quietly bypassed rather than punished — for now.

title: Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr
body: The settlement that refused was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer to the Company's agent survives only in his paraphrase: that the hill was not hers to sell and not his to buy.

title: The road around Doire mhòr
body: The Company opens its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and runs its cart-road around Doire mhòr's fields rather than through them.

title: Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lit
body: The first of the new beacons is finished on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg, a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower, with a Ròdaich keeper, paid for by the Company. Torcall Clachair builds it; James Fenn sets its lens.

title: The first keeper of Tobar dhearg
body: The first keeper of the southern beacon is Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg village, a fisherman's widow, who climbs the tower twice a night for the rest of her life. The village takes the keepership as a trust and keeps it in its own families through the age.

title: Raiders in the north-western waters
body: A Company brig is boarded off the north-west coast and stripped of her cargo of tools. The raiders are never identified; the Administration blames the custodians of the coast, and the custodians say the waters there have always had their own law.

title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
body: Samuel Wren copies the inscription on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag and sends it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall. No reply is recorded. The custodians tell him the stone is older than the Ròdaich and that nobody living can read it.

title: The currency reform
body: Human coinage is introduced alongside traditional barter, ostensibly for convenience. Within a decade it is the only accepted form of payment for anything requiring imported tools.

title: The mark and its hundred pence
body: The coins are struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped in from an Tìr Thall: the mark and its hundred pence. The first issue bears a ship on one face and nothing Rodian on either.

title: Cathair mhòr refuses the mark
body: The market of Cathair mhòr, the largest in the hills east of the capital, refuses the humans' coin for a full year. The custodians of the town give way when the Company's tool-sellers refuse to cross their bridge.

title: Two books at the capital market
body: At Cathair dhearg's market, tool-sellers take only marks, while cloth and fish still go by barter. The custodians' clerks begin keeping two sets of books, and complain of it in both.

title: Wren's winter at Dùn thais
body: At Dùn thais the masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh receive Samuel Wren for a winter of disputation. He asks them why the vein should be holy; they ask him why his fuel should be burned. Neither account of the winter records a winner.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg rebuilt
body: Company masons rebuild the old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg in dressed stone, wide enough for ore-carts to pass two abreast.

title: The Harbour Articles
body: A second agreement, the Harbour Articles, fixes dues and anchorages at Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. Like the first treaty it is written in the humans' tongue only, and this time two custodians refuse to sign.

title: The fishermen of Baile ghlas
body: The fishermen of Baile ghlas, whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain since anyone could remember, are charged anchorage under the Harbour Articles. They move their catch to their own small harbour and sell it there to anyone but the Company.

title: The northern concession
body: The council grants the Administration upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who will not work in the pits. The grant is for grazing; the families build houses of stone.

title: Death of Tormod mac Ailein
body: The high custodian who signed the first treaty dies at Cathair dhearg. The council chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh to follow him, a man who had never met a human before the Crossing and had dealt with little else since.

title: Harrow lost at sea
body: Edmund Harrow's ship does not return from the western crossing. The Company passes wholly into Thomas Pike's hands, and the humans' letter-books mourn Harrow as the man who found Rodos.

title: The Small-Burning Law lapses
body: Centuries of measured restraint end within a single generation. No formal repeal is recorded — it simply stops being enforced once it stops being profitable to enforce.

title: The last count at Doire mhin
body: The custodians of Doire mhin keep the old count of the Small-Burning Law, the measure of ore that might be burned in a year, one season longer than anyone else. The count is entered in their roll with the note that nobody asked for it.

title: A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg
body: A custodian of Dùn dhearg, Fionnghal nic Artair, writes a defence of the Small-Burning Law addressed to the council. It is the only such defence to survive. It argues that the Law was never about the ore but about the people who would become whatever the burning made them.

title: Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preaches that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon is copied and carried to the camps, where it is the first Ròdaich text the Company's agents are told to confiscate.

title: The spirits' priests of Achadh naomh
body: The priests of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach at Achadh naomh, in the hills north of the workings, refuse to light their hearths with ore bought from the Company. They burn peat, as their grandparents did, and teach that ore burned for wages is ore burned without the ancestors' leave.

title: Burning by the cartload
body: The Company's furnaces at Muileann chrom burn ore by the cartload to drive the new pumps, and the custodians' tally of what the hill may give in a year is not consulted. Coinneach Glas's council asks for the tally to be observed and receives a copy of the Company's accounts instead.

title: Henry Maddox Commissioner
body: Josiah Pell sails home to an Tìr Thall and does not come back. His successor, Henry Maddox, arrives with instructions to double the yield and a letter from the Company promising him a share of it.

title: The oaks of Cathair fhada
body: Maddox buys the oak woods around Cathair fhada for pit-props. The woods had been cut sparingly by the town for generations. They are gone within the working life of the men who felled them.

title: The first mining deaths blamed on speed
body: A tunnel collapse, worked faster than any Rodian crew would have chosen to work it, kills eleven. It is recorded as an accident.

title: The eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich
body: The collapse was at Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a gallery driven forward without the timbering the Ròdaich crews had asked for. The custodians' roll names all eleven dead. The Company's report names none and calls the gallery "unsound ground."

title: The coughing sickness
body: A dry cough runs through the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, worst among the boys who break ore at the pit-mouth. Thirty-eight die of it. The Mission's surgeon calls it a winter complaint; it lasts through the summer.

title: The orphans of Cill thais
body: The village of Cill thais takes in children orphaned by the coughing sickness, and keeps a house for them paid for by its own custodians. The Company, asked for a contribution, sends a crate of Mission primers.

title: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal lit
body: The second beacon is lit on the eastern shore at Baile ìseal. Torcall Clachair, too old now to climb, directs its building from a chair at the foot of the headland.

title: The keepers of Baile ìseal
body: The keepers of the eastern beacon are drawn from the fishing families of Baile ìseal. The town's custodians ask for, and get, a rule that the lamp will be lowered on the nights the boats go out to the deep grounds, so the fish will not be frightened. The rule lapses without anyone recording when.

title: The camp at Àth ìseal
body: The Company founds a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, at the ford below the new workings, for crews brought in from the coast. It is the first settlement on Rodos built for no purpose but the pit.

title: Doire mhòr's water taken
body: The Company diverts the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash ore at Cnoc fhiadhaich. No order is recorded; the stream is simply dammed one season and not released. Beathag Dhubh's people carry water by hand for two summers and then begin to leave.

title: The short hunger in the hills
body: With men drawn from the farms into the pits, the hill villages of Muileann chrom lose their oat harvest to rain nobody was home to cut ahead of. The Company sells meal at the camp stores for marks; the villages have few.

title: Meal-carts at Doire fhiadhaich
body: The villages of Doire fhiadhaich in the south send carts of meal north to the hill villages, as the old custom of the Holy Age required in a hungry year. The Company's agents at Àth ìseal buy up two of the carts on the road.

title: Mass excavation begins in earnest
body: The mountain is worked by the ton for the first time in Rodian history, for purposes no Rodian tradition would have chosen.

title: Rope for the winding-gear
body: The rope-walks of Dùn chrom, which had made cable for fishing boats, turn over entirely to winding-rope for the pit-heads. The Company pays well, and the town grows by half.

title: The Company's second charter
body: The Company is rechartered in an Tìr Thall with new capital and a new name the Ròdaich never adopt. Its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumber the Administration's own clerks four to one.

title: Barges at Cidhe Beag
body: Ore barges begin loading at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, floating the black ore downriver to the coast. The old canoe landing, used since before the Sundering, is widened with cut stone and its shrine moved uphill.

title: Abhainn uaine silts black
body: The washing of ore upstream silts Abhainn uaine with a black slurry, and the salmon runs at its mouth fail within a few seasons. The river's Ròdais name, the green river, is kept, and the fishermen use it bitterly.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain a barge town
body: Baile Mòr dhomhain, on the river road, grows into the busiest barge town of the north as the ore comes down to it from Cidhe Beag. Its population doubles, mostly with bargemen from the coast.

title: Baile dhomhain raised as a camp town
body: A second camp, Baile dhomhain, is laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdaich town drawn on paper before it was built. It is housing four hundred within two seasons.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr reopens
body: The old carters' house at the halfway stage of the ore road between the capital and the hills is rebuilt, and keeps the name An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. Its first keeper, Seònaid Bhàn, takes both marks and barter and is the only innkeeper on the road who will.

title: The carters of Doire chaol
body: The carters of Doire chaol, on the road just east of the capital, form a guild to bargain with the Company over rates for hauling ore. It is the first Ròdaich guild formed in the age, and the Company recognizes it because it is cheaper than breaking it.

title: Seann Toll made an ore port
body: The Company takes over the harbour at Seann Toll, below the workings, and builds a loading stage there. The town's fishing boats are moved to the next cove.

title: The first Rodian overseer appointed
body: A Ròdaich is given authority over other Rodian miners, answerable to human administrators — the first visible fracture within Rodian society itself, not just between it and the humans.

title: Raghnall Maor
body: The first overseer is Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader who had worked the pits since the first contract. He is given the Company's staff and a house with a slate roof, and from this office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward.

title: The overseers multiply
body: Within a few years there are overseers at every working in the district, all Ròdaich, all answerable to the Company's agents. The custodians' roll stops recording their names and records only their number.

title: Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr
body: The overseer of the new pits at Cnoc mhòr, Seumas Dubh, is killed by his own crew after a boy is crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried. The Company hangs two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging carried out by the Administration on Rodos.

title: Hawk-priests barred from the camps
body: Henry Maddox bars the priests of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig from the camps, on the ground that their preaching slows the work. The order is enforced by the overseers. Several of them are hawk-faithful themselves, and the roll says so.

title: The pox at Ros dhomhain
body: A spotted pox comes ashore on a Company ship at Ros dhomhain and moves up the ore road into the camps. The Mission counts four hundred and six dead; the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list.

title: The pox in the south
body: The pox spreads south from the harbour to Baile chiar and the villages round it. The custodians there keep a list of the dead on the lintel of the council house, cut into the stone, and it can still be read.

title: Baile dhìreach loses its harbour dues
body: The Administration moves its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and ends the division of harbour dues. The mixed council, left with half an income, cuts its members from six to four.

title: Arthur Lisle Commissioner
body: Henry Maddox leaves Rodos a rich man. Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, replaces him, and his first act is to have every agreement since the first treaty copied into a single bound book.

title: A customs house at Ros gheal
body: Lisle opens a second customs house at Ros gheal on the northern coast, where hawk-faithful fishing towns had been trading with Company ships without paying dues. The customs officer is chased out of the town twice in his first year.

title: The Muileann chiar silver dispute
body: Human interests attempt to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few resources the Ròdaich successfully keep fully under their own control throughout this age.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich and the silver guild
body: The silver seam was held for the town by its guild of refiners, and the guild was led by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came she met them at the adit with the guild's whole membership and the guild's ledgers, and asked them to find the humans' name anywhere in either.

title: The Silver Compact
body: Arthur Lisle, reading the treaties closely, finds nothing in them that covers silver. He signs a compact with the silver guild leaving the seam to the town, the first document of the age in which the Ròdaich side keeps the better terms.

title: Seann Bhral the silver port
body: The silver guild sends its bars to the sea through the old port of Seann Bhral rather than the Company's quays, and pays the port's custodians in silver for the use of it. The Company does not object, having no ground in the compact to object on.

title: The carters of Baile gheal
body: The carters of Baile gheal in the south-west take up the long haul of Seann Warr salt to the capital, a trade the Company does not bother to claim. It keeps the town's people out of the pits for the whole age.

title: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg lit
body: The third beacon is lit on the north-east coast at Àth dhearg. Its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, keeps a daybook of every ship he sees, and it is from his book that the number of human sailings in these years is known.

title: Àth dhearg builds the tower
body: The masons of the beacon at Àth dhearg are townsmen of Àth dhearg, paid half in marks and half in the promise that the tower will guide their own boats home. Tormod mac Pheadair, the keeper, is one of them.

title: Pirates off the eastern coast
body: A Company ore ship is taken off the eastern coast by raiders in low black boats and burned to the waterline, cargo and all. The Company says the raiders were paid by the silver guild. The silver guild says nothing.

title: A cove burned near Ceann leathan
body: A Company gunboat hunts the raiders to a cove near Ceann leathan and burns every boat drawn up on the shingle there. Most of them belonged to the town's fishermen. The raiders are not found.

title: The end of the joint council
body: The mixed council of Baile dhìreach breaks up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and is not reconvened. The human families move to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Ròdaich families stay. Those households that were both split or went quiet, and the record does not say which.

title: The boatyard moves to Inis chrom
body: The human boatbuilders of Baile dhìreach move their yard to Inis chrom, a day's sail east, where the Company has promised them timber. The town takes them in without a joint council or any other arrangement, and the record of their presence there fades within a generation.

title: The dry year in the east
body: Rain fails over the eastern farmlands around Achadh shean for a single season. It is remembered afterward as a warning nobody heeded, since the next dry spell, long after, came three years together.

title: Baile ruadh loses its seed
body: At Baile ruadh in the east the dry season kills the seed corn in the ground, and the town borrows seed from the Company's store at Seann Dunn at a price paid back over five harvests. It is the first Ròdaich town to owe the Company a debt in grain.

title: Aonghas mac Coinnich's question
body: At Dùn thais the Deer master Aonghas mac Coinnich puts a question to his students that the school's register calls new: why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore that every Ròdaich child sees. He does not answer it, and the register notes that he said it was the wrong question.

title: The Deer students of Baile Mòr uaine
body: Students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carry his question to Baile Mòr uaine and teach it in the town's hall of disputation. The hall's record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves and ends, like his, without an answer.

title: Cathair gheal on the concession
body: The human families of the northern concession found a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel. Its charter is issued by the Administration without reference to the custodians.

title: Human farms at Cnoc ghorm
body: Human farmers of the concession clear land beside the Ròdaich village of Cnoc ghorm, in the upland north-west, and build a mill. The villagers sell them grain until the mill is working and then stop.

title: A fishing station at Ceann mhòr
body: A few human fishing families of the concession settle at Ceann mhòr, the harbour under the north-western headland. They are the first humans to fish the island's waters for a living rather than for the Company's table.

title: The first Rodian child sent abroad
body: A single family, hoping to secure better treatment, sends a son to be educated in the humans' home country. He is never recorded returning.

title: The family of Eachann Mòr
body: The family that sent its son away was that of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his place on the council. The boy, Calum, sailed west on a Company ship with a letter of introduction from the Mission and a purse of marks.

title: The Mission school
body: The Mission opens a school at Ros dhomhain for Ròdaich children, taught in the humans' tongue. It takes thirty pupils in its first year, most of them the children of overseers.

title: Schooling at Inis bhàn
body: The custodians of Inis bhàn in the north open a school of their own in answer to the Mission's, teaching the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills. The Mission complains that the pupils come to its own school the next year already knowing how to argue.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: The Company rebuilds the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn to carry the eastern ore road. For as long as the carts run, it is the busiest crossing on that side of the island.

title: Ore through Inis bheag
body: Ore from the eastern workings is carted over the new bridge and down to the harbour of Inis bheag for shipment. The harbour is deepened by the Company, and the town's old fish market is moved to make room for the ore stage.

title: Baile mhin ships the eastern ore
body: The harbour of Baile mhin on the north-eastern coast takes the overflow of eastern ore that Inis bheag cannot load. The townsfolk are paid by the barge and the town builds its first stone houses on the proceeds.

title: Caol gharbh bypassed
body: The ore road to Inis bheag passes Caol gharbh by a mile, and the town, which had hoped for the traffic, gets only its dust. Its custodians write that they had not known a town could be damaged by a road it was not on.

title: The thing in the north-western sea
body: The crew of a Company brig report a beast larger than their ship off the north-western headlands. The Administration's clerk files the report with the complaints about pirates, and the Ròdaich sailors of the coast say they had wondered when the humans would see it.

title: Surveyors lost at Doire uaine
body: Two Company surveyors go up into the hills at Doire uaine against the advice of the villagers and are not seen again. The Company sends a search party, which comes back after a day and refuses to go further.

title: The offerings at Doire uaine
body: The villagers of Doire uaine leave offerings of salt and ore at the foot of the hills after the surveyors are lost, as they had in their grandparents' time after any death on the high ground. The Company forbids ore to be left lying and has the offerings collected, and the villagers change to salt alone.

title: The tithe increase
body: The portion of mined obsidian claimed by human administrators rises sharply, with no corresponding rise in what Rodian communities receive.

title: Lisle's tithe schedule
body: The new schedule is issued at the Residency over Arthur Lisle's signature, raising the Administration's portion from one part in five to one part in three. The custodians receive a copy in the humans' tongue and a translation made by a Mission pupil.

title: Weighing the grain at Dùn fhiadhaich
body: At Dùn fhiadhaich the tithe-collectors begin weighing grain as well as ore, on the ground that the town's farms feed the pits and share in the pits' profit. The custodians' roll calls this the tithe on the tithe.

title: The flux at Ros dhomhain
body: A bloody flux breaks out in the crowded quarters at the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission's nurse, Anne Colby, sets up a sick-house in the chapel, and the record credits her with keeping the dead to under two hundred.

title: The flux reaches Seann Vell
body: The flux spreads to Seann Vell, the port a little east along the coast, carried by the ore barges. The custodians of the town close the barge landing for a season and are fined for it by the Company.

title: Walter Crane Commissioner
body: Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency of a fever of the heart. Walter Crane, who had been the Company's chief agent at the pits, is appointed Commissioner in his place, the first to hold both offices in succession.

title: The pay office at Ceann mhin
body: Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings to Ceann mhin, and has the crews walk there to be paid rather than send the paymaster to them. The walk is a day each way. The crews are not paid for it.

title: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor
body: Raghnall Maor dies, and the Company gives his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The overseer's office, which the custodians had hoped would lapse with the man, becomes a family's inheritance.

title: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag lit
body: The fourth beacon is lit on the northern shore at Muileann bheag. It is the first to burn ore instead of oil, and the keepers report that its flame throws a colour on the water no oil lamp ever did.

title: The fishermen of Muileann bheag
body: The fishermen of Muileann bheag complain that the ore flame of the new beacon casts a colour on the water that drives the herring off. The keepers do not change the lamp. The herring come back within a season, and the complaint is withdrawn in a letter that the Company keeps.

title: The dig at Làrach an Teampaill
body: The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe digs at Làrach an Teampaill for a season with Company labourers, looking for proof of an older faith on the island. He finds cut stone, burnt bone and marks he cannot read, and writes that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agree, and add nothing.

title: The pillar at Cnoc chiar
body: Edwin Lowe copies the inscription on the pillar near Cnoc chiar and compares it with Wren's copy of the obelisk at Cnoc bheag. He decides the two scripts are not the same and that neither is Ròdaich. His notes stop there.

title: The column at Cnoc ghorm
body: Lowe's last copy is of the column near Cnoc ghorm, and he writes beside it that its marks resemble the pillar's but not closely enough to help. He leaves Rodos the next year, and his notebooks go with him.

title: The silver guild refuses again
body: A Company agent, Martha Gale, offers the silver guild of Muileann chiar a partnership, on terms the guild's ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, now very old, has the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall and then refused by show of hands.

title: The camp at Achadh dhomhain
body: A new camp is opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries under the hill, and within a few seasons it is the most crowded settlement in the district. Its houses are built of spoil.

title: Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar
body: The weavers of Dùn chiar take a Company contract to supply canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the ore. The town prospers on it, and its custodians note that it is the first time the town has made anything for a use it did not approve of.

title: The first of the immortal generation
body: A child born into the mining camps is exposed to more raw ore across her lifetime than any Rodian in living memory — and does not age the way the people around her do. Her name is Aisling.

title: The ore weighed at the quay
body: The Company installs a great steelyard at the Ros dhomhain quay, and from now on the island's yield is known by the ton and the hundredweight. The custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, stops being entered in the roll.

title: Ros dhìreach the second ore port
body: The Company opens a second ore stage at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast for the workings south of the hills. Its first cargo is lost in a squall off the harbour mouth, and the fishermen who had been moved to make room for the stage refuse to go out after it.

title: The condition goes unnamed
body: Whatever is happening to the child born two years earlier has no word yet, in any language spoken on the island. It will be decades before anyone tries to coin one.

title: The shrine at Cill dhìreach
body: At Cill dhìreach, a village on the edge of the workings, the custodians keep a small shrine where the pit crews leave the first piece of ore of each new gallery. The Company tolerates the custom because it costs a stone a gallery.

title: The keepers of Cill ghlas
body: The custodians of the shrine at Cill ghlas, in the hills among the workings, keep the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the Company's pits deepen around them. It is the last shrine in the district still visited on the old feast days by the pit crews.

title: A' Phlàigh Uaine
body: The Green Death moves through the mining camps — the ore dust itself is blamed, though no formal study is ever completed. Twenty-six settlements record cases.

title: The first cases at Achadh dhomhain
body: The Green Death is first noticed at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brings up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buries forty in its first month, in a field outside the spoil-heaps that is still called the green acre.

title: Twenty-six settlements
body: The sickness spreads along the ore roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and falls hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. The custodians' roll lists the twenty-six settlements that record cases and leaves a blank line after the last, as if expecting another.

title: The Green Death at Baile chrom
body: The Green Death reaches Baile chrom in the hills, not the town of the same name in the north-west. The record distinguishes them with care, because in later years the names become confused in the retelling of the island's hungers.

title: Àth ghlas burns its huts
body: At Àth ghlas the custodians order every hut in which a death has occurred burned with its bedding. The Company protests the loss of its property. The custodians note that the sickness stops at Àth ghlas sooner than anywhere else.

title: The dead of Cnoc naomh
body: At Cnoc naomh the dead of the Green Death are buried in the churchyard of the town's old shrine until the ground is full, and then in a field outside it. The field is never ploughed again.

title: Doctor Bright's study
body: The Administration's physician, Nathaniel Bright, begins a study of the sickness at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. He falls ill in the second season of his work, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table.

title: Walter Crane dies of the Green Death
body: Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps during the worst of the sickness, dies of it at the Residency. The Company's agent at Ros dhomhain, Martha Gale, holds his seal for the months until a successor arrives.

title: George Tolley Commissioner
body: George Tolley arrives from an Tìr Thall with orders that the yield must not fall because of the sickness. He does not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Ròdaich custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.

title: Quarantine at Caol mhin
body: Tolley sets up a quarantine station at Caol mhin on the northern coast for ships arriving from an Tìr Thall, holding them offshore until their crews are inspected. It is the first order of his administration the Ròdaich approve of, and they say so.

title: The camps turn to the hawk
body: With the hawk-priests still barred from the camps, their sermons are carried in by the crews themselves. The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a disciplinary matter.

title: Anne Colby's sick-houses
body: Anne Colby opens sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nurses there until the sickness ebbs. She is the only human the camp people name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.

title: The huts of Cnoc gharbh
body: Cnoc gharbh, whose people had worked the southern galleries, abandons its camp huts after the sickness and moves back to the old village on the hill. The Company rebuilds the huts the next year and brings in crews from the west.

title: The first work-refusal strike
body: An entire mining settlement halts extraction for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years prior. It ends when food supplies, controlled by human administrators, run out.

title: The strike at Baile thais
body: The settlement was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the halt was called by the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn after the Company refused to close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no ore left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty.

title: The Company's granary
body: After the strike the Company builds a granary of its own at Muileann chrom and forbids the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration. The order is enforced by the overseers and signed by Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor.

title: Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh
body: The fishermen of Ros gharbh carry salt fish up to the camps by night, past the Company's granary rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of the decade that ran in the right direction.

title: Catrìona goes to the silver town
body: Turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit, Catrìona nic Eachainn goes east to Muileann chiar, where the silver guild takes her on as a refiner. The Company asks for her to be sent back. The guild's reply is filed but not preserved.

title: The springs at Muileann ruadh
body: The Administration builds a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for officials recovering from fevers. Ròdaich who had bathed there for centuries are admitted on certain days and charged a penny.

title: Muileann chiar expands
body: The silver town grows alongside the obsidian operation, human demand for both metals accelerating extraction the reverent tradition never would have permitted.

title: A second Muileann chiar
body: The growth of the silver trade crowds the old town, and the guild founds a daughter settlement to the west for its refiners and carters, which takes the same name. The record calls them the old town and the new, and does not always say which it means.

title: Silver for marks
body: The silver guild begins selling bar silver to the Company for marks at a price the guild fixes. It is the only commodity on Rodos in the age priced by Ròdaich hands, and the guild's hall fills with human coin.

title: Silversmiths at Muileann bhàn
body: Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn on the road to the silver town and make a living working the guild's bar into ornaments for the humans' market. Their work is the one Ròdaich craft sold in an Tìr Thall under a Ròdaich name.

title: The Dark Unicorn blesses the coin
body: The priests of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, bless the Residency's new coin at Tolley's request. The dualist priesthood teaches that the dark and the light each have their due; the dissenting priests say the coin is only one of them.

title: The second currency reform
body: Rodian barter goods are formally devalued against human coinage a second time, on terms set entirely by the human administration.

title: Wool devalued at Baile Mòr fhionn
body: At Baile Mòr fhionn, where wool had been the measure of every bargain, a fleece is now worth by the Residency's table what a half-fleece was worth before. The town's weavers stop bringing wool to market and send it overseas on their own account, until the Company refuses them freight.

title: The boats of Caol fhiadhaich sold
body: The fishing fleet of Caol fhiadhaich, unable to pay the new harbour dues in marks, sells half its boats to the Company. The men who sailed them go into the pits under the next year's contracts.

title: The dissenters go to Cnoc bheag
body: Priests of the Dark Unicorn who refused the blessing leave the capital's temple and settle in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. Their community there keeps the older reading of the dual faith, and becomes a place where custodians who have lost their seats are received.

title: Iain Maor
body: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor dies, and his son Iain takes the overseer's staff. Iain Maor is the first overseer to have been schooled at the Mission; he keeps his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais.

title: The Levy
body: Tolley issues an ordinance, the Levy, requiring every farming village in the west and north to send one in five of its able adults to the pits for a term of two years. The villages are compensated in marks, at the new rate.

title: Levy officers at Caol mhòr
body: The Levy's officers take their first quota at Caol mhòr in the north-west, reading the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue. The custodians of the town take down the names again in Ròdais, so that they will know whom to look for.

title: The Levy in the north-west
body: The Levy falls hardest on the villages around Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Ròdaich of the concession are taken; the human farmers of the concession are exempt.

title: Baile ìseal sends its people
body: Baile ìseal sends forty-one of its people to the pits under the Levy. Nineteen come back when their term ends. The custodians' roll gives the names of the other twenty-two and the camps they were sent to.

title: Muileann naomh buys its way out
body: The custodians of Muileann naomh pay the Levy's officers in silver to reduce the town's quota by half. The officers take the silver and the full quota. The complaint is lodged at the Residency and filed.

title: The Deer school's hall closed
body: George Tolley closes the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Dùn thais, citing a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the ore's colour is a kind of sickness. The masters go on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year.

title: The last disputation at Doire chiar
body: At Doire chiar, a Deer village north of the eastern workings, the masters hold the last public disputation of the school in the open air, in the village's threshing-floor. Its subject is whether a question may be forbidden. The Administration's clerk who attends records that it may.

title: Teaching in the sacred forest
body: Masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh who can no longer teach in a hall begin teaching in the sacred forest near Muileann chiar, under the trees, where the Administration has no building to close.

title: Building the last beacon at Baile chrom
