body: Work begins on the fifth and last beacon, on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, with masons drawn by the Levy from the same villages whose fields they leave unworked.

title: The masons of Cnoc thais
body: The masons of Cnoc thais are taken by the Levy to build the beacon at Baile chrom. Their foreman, Dùghall Clachair, cuts the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room. It is the only inscription on any of the five towers.

title: The five lighthouses complete
body: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg — the full ring of coastal beacons is finished, built to serve trade that is by now extraction in every way but name.

title: Cuan ruadh loses its trade
body: With the ring of beacons finished, Company steamers round the island without stopping, and the old coastal trade of Cuan ruadh, which had carried goods up and down the eastern shore, dies within a few years.

title: Taigh-solais Baile chrom lit
body: The beacon at Baile chrom is lit with an ore flame, completing the ring. The Company's ships can now round the island by night, and the keepers' daybooks record the sailings doubling in the next few years.

title: Gorta Baile chrom
body: The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, worsened by a mining workforce too depleted by mass conscription to farm its own land.

title: Baile chrom goes hungry
body: The hunger is worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. The custodians record that more died there than in any other settlement, and the Administration, which kept its own count, does not dispute the figure.

title: The hunger at Doire ghlas
body: At Doire ghlas in the north the hunger takes the old and the very young first. The village sends its young to the camps for the Company's rations and is half empty by the end of the year.

title: Inis mhin eats its seed
body: At Inis mhin on the north coast the townsfolk eat their seed corn in the second winter of the hunger. The Mission kitchen at the harbour feeds three hundred a day for a season.

title: The hunger reaches Seann Bhrenn
body: The hunger reaches as far east as Seann Bhrenn, where the custodians open the old grain-pits of the Holy Age, which had not been filled in living memory. They are found to hold only dust.

title: The relief ship
body: A relief ship with grain from an Tìr Thall is held at Ros dhomhain for a month while the Residency and the Company argue over who is to pay for its unloading. The Mission opens kitchens at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom meanwhile, and Anne Colby, returned to the island, runs the one at Baile chrom.

title: The Levy suspended
body: The Levy is suspended in the famine districts, too late for the harvest. It is not repealed. The custodians note that it was never used again, and that it never needed to be, since the villages had learned what it meant.

title: Cnoc mhòr walks south
body: The families of Cnoc mhòr in the north walk south to the camps rather than starve, and take work under the Company. Their village stands empty for a generation.

title: Robert Haskins Commissioner
body: George Tolley retires with honours. Robert Haskins, his successor, orders that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, then sets the tithe before the council has met.

title: Customs at Seann Dunn
body: Haskins opens a customs house at Seann Dunn on the eastern coast and a Company store with it. The store sells the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers hold the debts of half the district.

title: The first organized petition
body: Rodian custodians, for the first time acting jointly rather than settlement by settlement, submit a formal grievance to the human administration. It is not answered.

title: The conclave at Ceann àrsaidh
body: The petition was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians from nineteen settlements, meeting for the first time as one body. It was carried to the Residency by the custodian of Cill ghlas, a woman named Peigi Ghlas, and handed to a clerk.

title: Àth fhionn signs
body: The custodian of Àth fhionn in the south-east, Ruairidh mac Thormoid, is the oldest of those who signed the petition. He had been born before the humans' coin was struck, and he says so beside his signature.

title: Resentment first recorded
body: The earliest surviving Ròdaich grievance texts date from this period — not yet organized resistance, but the first written acknowledgment that something has gone wrong.

title: Leabhar Baile thais
body: The earliest grievance text to survive is a book of complaints kept at Baile thais, set down by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. The custodians' copyists call it Leabhar Baile thais.

title: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd
body: The poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of ore at Muileann dhearg since boyhood, makes songs of the Levy and the famine that are sung in the camps. The overseers forbid them, and the prohibition is the reason several of them were written down.

title: Songs at An Taigh-òsta Grianach
body: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd are sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach becomes known for them. The Company's carters sing them too, the keeper records, without always knowing what they are singing.

title: The Company's deep-water quay
body: The Company builds a deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain able to take the new iron steamships, which burn the island's own ore to carry it away. Fearchar Bàrd makes a song of that, and it is the one of his most often quoted.

title: The deep quay at Ceann chaol
body: A second deep-water quay is built at Ceann chaol in the south-east for the eastern ore. Its builders are brought from the coast, and the town, which had been a village of forty houses, is a town of four hundred.

title: Baile thais walls its pithead
body: The Company rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a gate, with a watchman paid to keep count of who goes in. It is the first working on Rodos to be walled against its own crews.

title: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at the silver town
body: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at Muileann chiar, a refiner of the silver guild to the end. The camp people of Baile thais send a delegation to her burying, and the Company docks each of them a day's pay.

title: The quay fire
body: A fire starts in the Company's ore sheds at Ros dhomhain and burns for three days, taking two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's investigation finds no cause; the harbour quarter's own account has several.

title: The council meets without a high custodian
body: The Council of Custodians fails to agree on a new high custodian after the death of the last, and sits for years with the seat empty. Robert Haskins writes to an Tìr Thall that this makes the council easier to deal with.

title: Tiormachd Achadh shean
body: The Long Drought settles over the island's dry season for three consecutive years, straining a population already stretched thin by extraction quotas.

title: The wells of Achadh shean
body: At Achadh shean, whose name the drought bears, the wells fail in the second summer and the cattle are driven west in a column that the roll says was a day long. Fewer than half of them reach water.

title: The dry country
body: Ten districts of the east are counted as drought country by the custodians' roll, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration keeps no count of its own.

title: The cattle of Baile chaol
body: At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought rather than watched to die. The salted meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.

title: Doire fhionn walks for water
body: At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk to the spring at Àth ruadh and back each day for water, a journey of half a day. The custodians record this for the three dry years and then stop recording it.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, keeps running through all three dry years. Pilgrims of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach come to it from across the east, and the Administration posts a watchman to charge them for the water. He is recalled after a single season.

title: The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine
body: Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the town's people feed them without charge, as the old spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.

title: Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh
body: A fever of bad water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Two hundred and sixty die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause correctly.

title: The fever at Cnoc shean
body: The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, where the town's single well is found to be tainted. The custodians close it and the town drinks from carts for a year.

title: The Mission's wells
body: The Mission digs deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall. They hold. The custodians of the east record the Mission's wells alongside the Company's quotas, without comment, on facing pages.

title: Achadh chaol goes to the pits
body: The people of Achadh chaol in the north-east, their fields burned out by the drought, go to the pits for wages. They are the first villagers of the eastern farming country to do so, and their custodian records it as the end of the village rather than a move.

title: The quota not lowered
body: The ore quota is not lowered during the drought. The custodians of the east petition Haskins singly, since the joint petition had not been answered; he replies to each that the matter is under consideration.

title: The petition of Àth mhòr
body: The custodian of Àth mhòr, Iseabail nic Leòid, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages cataloguing her town's dead animals. Haskins replies in two lines. Both documents survive, bound together by a later clerk.

title: The first mixed-blood inheritance dispute
body: A legal case over whether a child of one Rodian and one human parent may inherit customary mining rights sets a precedent the administration writes entirely to its own benefit.

title: The case of Thomas Hale
body: The child in the case was Thomas Hale, a grandson of the Baile dhìreach marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Ròdaich grandmother. The magistrate at Ros dhomhain, Oliver Dunstan, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration recognizes, and that it recognizes only its own.

title: Dunstan's rule applied
body: Within a few years Dunstan's ruling has been used to transfer eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each on the ground that some owner in the line had married a human or been born to one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.

title: A cutting at Cnoc dhubh transferred
body: Among the cuttings transferred under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by the same family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother in the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.

title: The Lamp-Watch
body: A society of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins meeting at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known act is to pay for the burial of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.

title: Edward Vane Commissioner
body: Robert Haskins is recalled after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths. Edward Vane replaces him. Vane is the first Commissioner to have been born on Rodos, at the Residency, and he speaks Ròdais badly, but at all.

title: The tram-road to Ros dhìreach
body: Vane lays an iron tram-road from the southern workings down to the ore port at Ros dhìreach, drawn by mules. It halves the cost of shipping ore and ends the carting trade of the villages along the old road.

title: The night-shift order
body: Extraction is extended to run continuously, day and night, for the first time — the mountain given no season of rest at all.

title: The night crews at Cnoc chaol
body: The order is felt first at Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by ore-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll records that the hill was given no silence at all, and then leaves the rest of the page blank.

title: The night-shift strike
body: The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift and are replaced within a week by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch pays the strikers' families for a season and runs out of money.

title: The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain
body: The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them away from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.

title: Matthew Dunne's sermon
body: The Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, Matthew Dunne, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Ròdaich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission. Dunne is recalled to an Tìr Thall, and the sermon is copied by the Lamp-Watch and read in the camps.

title: The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol
body: A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death, it kills slowly. The Company pays a pension to widows for a year, then stops.

title: Iain Maor and the night shift
body: Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was reversed a month later for want of anyone else.

title: Ore-lamps from Baile ghorm
body: The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own record notes that they are the first lamps ever made on the island for work in the dark by order.

title: Fionnan born
body: A second child manifests the same unprecedented bonding Aisling did half a century earlier. The exposure is not a one-time accident. It is an ongoing industrial condition.

title: The Administration's census
body: The Administration counts the people of Rodos by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are precise to the household; its figures for the Ròdaich are round to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.

title: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the Deer masters
body: The last master of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh to teach openly in the colonial age, Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, dies at Dùn thais. No successor is named, and the school's register ends with her death. It will be taken up again only long after the humans are gone.

title: The custodians' records at Muileann chaol
body: The custodians of the east begin sending copies of their rolls to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, for safekeeping, away from the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families and kept in a cellar.

title: The second Muileann chaol
body: Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by error to the smaller town of the same name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians' record of them notes that they were kept just as well.

title: The word finally coined
body: Facing two confirmed cases, Rodian custodians settle on a term for what's happening: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood" — rendered in the humans' tongue as obsidian-touched. It is meant clinically. It will outlive that intention.

title: The custodians who named it
body: The word was agreed by a meeting of custodians held at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word for a medical register. The roll records the vote and does not record who proposed it.

title: The Administration's register
body: The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Ròdaich child showing the condition be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians comply by reporting none.

title: The third currency reform
body: Traditional Rodian barter is formally abolished as legal tender entirely. Every transaction on the island now runs through human coinage.

title: The barter houses closed
body: The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are closed by order. A clerk of the Residency notes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."

title: The fishwives of Inis mhòr
body: The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the harbour steps since before the Crossing, refuse to take coin for a week in protest at the barter houses' closing. They give their fish away instead. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.

title: Marks borrowed at interest
body: With barter abolished, the hill villages borrow marks from the Company's stores to buy seed, at interest. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.

title: The old market at Muileann òg
body: The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season. The ground stands empty until it is used, long after, for a fair.

title: Mòrag nic Iain Maor
body: Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her appointment in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."

title: Charles Merriman Commissioner
body: Edward Vane dies at the Residency. His successor, Charles Merriman, arrives with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Rodos.

title: The constable post at Muileann shean
body: Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern ore road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.

title: A barracks at Tobar ghorm
body: A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid a rent for the ground and uses it, the record notes, to buy the village out of its debts to the Company store.

title: A grey-night gathering at Baile chrom
body: The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom have been meeting at night in the fields to pray to a grey goose. The Mission cannot find the source of the practice and describes it as a superstition learned from the Ròdaich. The Ròdaich of Baile chrom disown it.

title: The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain
body: The dockers at Ros dhomhain, Ròdaich and human alike, refuse to load ore for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers join Ròdaich ones. Merriman's constables end it, and the human dockers are shipped west.

title: Seann Vell's dockers stay out
body: The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the ore diverted to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped west, having no humans among them, but they are not hired again either.

title: Lorccan born
body: A third case, born into a mining town rather than a mining camp — proof the phenomenon has outgrown any single site.

title: Cian born
body: A fourth, within a year of the third — the closest the immortal generation comes to being born in a cluster rather than a scatter.

title: Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas
body: The Company begins driving galleries under the hills around Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their request on his plan and sets the charges below it.

title: Powder landed at Caol ìseal
body: The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.

title: Scàineadh Cill ghlas
body: The Rending — a fault line tears open in the hills east of the capital, around Cill ghlas during a routine excavation, killing dozens and closing an entire mining district for a generation.

title: The first open confrontation
body: A mining accident, blamed by Rodian workers on human indifference to safety, becomes the first recorded violent clash between the two populations.

title: The shrine at Cill ghlas lost
body: The old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through the whole age, is swallowed by the Rending with its shrine. The custodians' roll records the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead, and a later copyist has corrected the order.

title: The district closed
body: The Company closes the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas and its hamlets without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to thorn.

title: Achadh chaol raised by the displaced
body: People of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, on the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement founded in the age by Ròdaich for Ròdaich without a Company surveyor's hand in it.

title: The clash at Muileann chrom
body: The accident that began the clash was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, in which seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable were killed.

title: Mòrag Maor at the inquiry
body: At the Administration's inquiry into the clash, the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor testifies that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her evidence is struck from the record. The Lamp-Watch obtains a copy of it anyway.

title: The grey fever
body: A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs across the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes with alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.

title: The grey fever at Cathair mhòr
body: At Cathair mhòr the grey fever closes the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll records the dead by street, and the longest list is the street where the carters lived.

title: The grey fever at Dùn thais
body: At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician who had been sent by the Administration to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The Deer masters' old houses are opened as sick-rooms.

title: The second organized petition
body: This one includes an implicit threat rather than a plea. It is the first Rodian document the human administration bothers to respond to — with increased security, not concessions.

title: The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach
body: The custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, Coinneach Ruadh, signs the second petition and is dismissed from his post as clerk to the Company store the same week. He is one of eleven signatories who lose Company work over it.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill
body: The second petition was drafted by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and a member of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders from thirty-one settlements. It ends with a sentence the Residency underlined: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked.

title: The constabulary enlarged
body: Merriman's answer is to triple the constabulary and post companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, with a fortified store at each. The constables are paid from the tithe.

title: Barracks at Dùn chrom
body: A constabulary barracks is built at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills, with room for two hundred men. It stands empty for most of its first year for want of constables to fill it.

title: Ìomhar Seabhag
body: At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag preaches that Mòd's hunger has turned toward those who have eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west begin to serve as meeting houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables do not yet know it.

title: The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal
body: At Ros gheal the hawk-faithful fishing families, who had chased out the Company's customs officers a century before, raise a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall. The constables order it down. It is rebuilt three times in a single season.

title: The hawk and the Deer at Inis bhàn
body: At Inis bhàn the priests of the hawk and a few who still keep the Deer school's questions in private meet for a disputation, the first between the two in living memory. The record calls it inconclusive, and notes that both sides afterward signed the petition.

title: The grey fever in the north-west
body: The grey fever returns and settles in the north-west, around Baile chrom and the concession towns, where it kills humans as readily as Ròdaich. The Mission's hospital at Cathair gheal overflows, and Ròdaich and human patients lie in the same wards for the first time.

title: Muileann fhionn shut in
body: Muileann fhionn, a Ròdaich mill town in the north-west, closes its roads against the fever and keeps them closed for a season. Human carters of the concession are turned back with their loads at the town's edge.

title: The fever at Tobar fhiadhaich
body: At Tobar fhiadhaich in the north the fever takes one household in three. The custodians of the village burn no huts, having heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time but judging it too late.

title: The taverns fortify
body: Roadside houses along the old mining routes begin doubling as informal militia waypoints — infrastructure quietly repurposing itself for a conflict not yet declared.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Òir
body: An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house on the eastern road beyond Dùn dhearg, digs a well in its yard and builds a wall round the well. The keeper tells the Company's carters it is against thieves.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, the roadside house on the northern road through the Deer country, takes on six new ostlers in a single season, none of whom know anything about horses.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach walled
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, known since the songs of Fearchar Bàrd as the singing house, raises a wall around its yard and puts a watch on its gate.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach barred
body: Am Buabhall Fortanach, the great roadside tavern on the south-western road, takes to barring its gates at dusk and keeping a watch on the roof. Its keeper, Tormod Buabhall, keeps a list of travellers that he sends up the road each week, to whom the record does not say.

title: The harbour of Doire shean
body: The little harbour of Doire shean, below Am Buabhall Fortanach, becomes the landing place for the goods the house cannot take by road. The fishermen of Doire shean are paid in silver from the east.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, on the northern road, the stables are rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men. The Company's carters notice that the loft is never empty and never has the same men in it.

title: An Sligeanach Fad' às
body: An Sligeanach Fad' às, on the eastern road near the silver country, becomes the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sends word from the camps to Muileann chiar. The silver guild pays its keeper's rent.

title: The runners of Àth fhiadhaich
body: Runners from Àth fhiadhaich carry the Lamp-Watch's letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town. They are boys of twelve and thirteen, too young to be stopped by constables.

title: Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers
body: The Lamp-Watch's ledgers of money received from the silver guild are kept at Achadh mhòr, a village near the house on the eastern road, in the roof of the village's shrine.

title: Seònaid's house
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house on the ore road reopened by Seònaid Bhàn in the early years of the extraction, is kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It is the busiest of the fortified houses, and the one the constables search most often and find least in.

title: The first coordinated work stoppage
body: Multiple mining regions halt extraction on the same day for the first time — proof that Rodian resistance, for all its scattering, could act as one when it chose to.

title: Muileann bheag in the north-east
body: The workings at Muileann bheag in the north-east, among the Deer villages, stop with the rest. The town's custodian writes that it was the first thing the town had done in concert with the hills in a hundred years.

title: The northern pits at Àth dhomhain
body: The pits north of the hills at Àth dhomhain stop with the rest on the day of the stoppage, having received the signal by a runner rather than the beacon. Their crew-leaders are among those shipped west.

title: Ceann bheag stops
body: The ore stage at Ceann bheag on the northern coast stops loading the same day. Its dockers had not been told of the stoppage in advance; they stop because the ore stops arriving.

title: The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal
body: The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal in the north-east, who cut stone for the Company's buildings, put down their tools on the day of the stoppage without being asked. Nobody in the record says why.

title: The day the pits stopped
body: On the day of the stoppage every working in the Muileann chrom district halted at once, together with Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The signal was a beacon fire lit on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.

title: The ore ships wait
body: The Company's steamships wait at Ros dhomhain for six days with empty holds. The agents at the quay write that they have never before seen the harbour so quiet, and that it frightened them more than the crowds.

title: The stoppage broken
body: The stoppage ends when the constables close the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders are arrested; thirty-two are released without charge, eight are shipped west to an Tìr Thall for trial and are not heard of again.

title: Beacon hill at Doire mhòr
body: Doire mhòr, which had refused the first contract and then lost its water, has by now only a few households. The beacon of the stoppage was lit on its hill by the descendants of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burn the hill's heather to deny it to them.

title: Fewer ships from the west
body: The keepers' daybooks at the five beacons record fewer ships arriving from an Tìr Thall each year, and the ships that come are older. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home that they do not describe.

title: Caol leathan's idle harbour
body: At Caol leathan the wool-ships for the humans' market wait for cargo space that does not come. The merchants of the town begin selling their wool inland again, by barter, which is illegal.

title: Caol bheag's empty quay
body: The Company's quay at Caol bheag on the northern coast, built for the eastern trade, handles one ship in a season. The Company's agent there writes that he has been forgotten.

title: Imperial overreach begins openly
body: Human administrators begin issuing directives with no Rodian counsel sought at all — the polite fiction of permission finally dropped.

title: Lionel Strake Commissioner
body: Charles Merriman leaves Rodos in ill health. Lionel Strake, a soldier, replaces him. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, makes no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he does not call on it.

title: The council locked out
body: Strake has the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians meet instead in the Dark Unicorn's temple, whose priests, who had blessed the humans' coin, now shelter those who had petitioned against it.

title: The confiscation edict
body: Human authorities formally claim the right to seize any Rodian dwelling deemed necessary for extraction expansion. It is the single most-cited grievance in every surviving account of what came next.

title: The seizure of Doire mhòr
body: The first dwellings taken under the edict are those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill. The last households are carried out by constables. The village that refused the first contract is the first to be emptied by the last.

title: Evictions at Baile dhomhain
body: At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets are pulled down for a spoil-tip. The families are offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for their timber; most go to kin in the hill villages instead.

title: Mòrag Maor lays down the staff
body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor, fourth of her line to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, refuses to carry out evictions in her district and breaks the staff at the Company's door. Three other overseers resign in the same month. The Company appoints humans to their places.

title: The silver guild arms
body: The silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact made a century before, begins buying rifles through the eastern pirates. Its ledger enters them as refining tools.

title: Rifles by way of the pirates
body: The rifles for the silver guild come ashore from the raiders' boats in the eastern waters, where no Company gunboat has patrolled for years. The raiders take payment in silver bar, by weight.

title: The council at Cnoc bheag forest
body: Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of the Dark Unicorn meet in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and form a single council for the mining regions. Eilidh nic Raghnaill is chosen to speak for it. The meeting is not recorded by any human source.

title: The arrest order
body: Strake orders the arrest of Eilidh nic Raghnaill and the members of the forest council. The constables go to Baile thais and find the house empty and the town silent.

title: War declared
body: Rodian resistance, coordinated for the first time across multiple mining regions, moves from grievance to open conflict.

title: The stores taken at Muileann chrom
body: The war opens in the hills. At Muileann chrom the fortified store is rushed at first light by crews under Mòrag nic Iain, and its eleven constables surrender without a shot fired. The store's rifles and its grain are carried off before noon.

title: The quay at Ceann fhada seized
body: Crews from the camps take the Company's ore quay at Ceann fhada and sink two barges across its mouth. No ore leaves the hills by water again in the age.

title: The siege of the store at Baile thais
body: At Baile thais the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days, the same span as the first strike a lifetime before. They surrender on the twelfth, when their water runs out. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed, an order the Residency did not expect and did not reciprocate.

title: The northern pits rise
body: The crews at Baile gharbh and the northern pits rise in the same week, take the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and send the constables south on foot.

title: The ore road cut
body: Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, closes the gates of the house across the ore road, and the men in its loft come down armed. The road between the capital and the hills is cut at its halfway stage and stays cut.

title: Uilleam Gobha's forge
body: At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha turns the Company's own blasting-powder into grenades cased in ore-tin, and forges pike-heads from rails torn up in the galleries. The rebels' council records that it could not have fought its first season without him.

title: The capital rises
body: At Cathair dhearg the custodians break the Residency's locks on their council hall and sit in it again. The townsfolk hold Drochaid Cathair dhearg against the constables sent up from the harbour, and the bridge built for ore-carts is barricaded with them.

title: Cathair dhomhain joins
body: At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk break open the Company's warehouse, the first building on Rodos the Company ever owned, and carry off its tools for the council's companies.

title: Muileann mhin takes sides
body: At Muileann mhin, a small port just east of the capital, the townsfolk argue for three days and then send boats to the council. The boats carry food up the coast to the capital through the winter.

title: The Residency fortified
body: Lionel Strake withdraws the Administration into the Residency above Ros dhomhain and fortifies the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below it, overwhelmingly Ròdaich, neither joins the rising nor opposes it, and the constables do not trust it enough to leave the walls.

title: The fight at the ford of Àth chiar
body: A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the ore road to relieve the hills and is met at the ford of Àth chiar. The rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back; the rebels lose nineteen, whose names the council's roll gives in full.

title: Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom
body: Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and stops at the barracks there for a night. In the morning the town has closed its gates behind them, and the column continues to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.

title: The silver town rises
body: The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury. The Company agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. It is the only place on the island where the rising took nothing, the guild's ledger notes, because the humans had never held anything there to take.

title: The surrender at Dùn ìseal
body: The small constabulary post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, surrenders to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.

title: Dùn dhearg declares
body: The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. It is the town whose custodian had written the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and the declaration quotes it.

title: Cnoc leathan's riflemen
body: Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and garrison the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are allowed to go home with their carts.

title: The eastern pits at Ros fhionn
body: The crews of the eastern workings around Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, letting the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there take ship for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern ore road falls silent.

title: Seann Toll shelled
body: A Company steamship shells the ore stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. It is the first time the humans turn the island's own ore, burning in their boilers, against a Ròdaich town.

title: Coaling at Inis mhòr
body: The Company steamships coal at Inis mhòr, the harbour just east of the capital's bay, from the ore stacked on its quay. Townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.

title: The fishermen of Seann Chwen
body: Fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company withdraws its coastal shipping to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.

title: The other Seann Chwen
body: The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, on the south coast further west, join the raids along the shore. The record keeps the two towns apart by naming their boats.

title: Cathair gheal behind its walls
body: The human town of Cathair gheal, on the northern concession, closes its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not reply.

title: Muileann àrsaidh closes its road
body: The concession town of Muileann àrsaidh closes its road with carts and keeps a watch on it, against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept for the rest of the war.

title: The hawk-shrines open
body: Ìomhar Seabhag declares from the shrine at Seann Skell that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. Hawk-shrines across the west become recruiting houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.

title: The hawk company at Seann Skell
body: The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, from which the human port of Ros bheag lies a short march to the south-west. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.

title: The southern beacon dark
body: The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal follow. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.

title: No relief from the west
body: The Administration's letter-books record repeated requests for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. One ship arrives in the whole first year of the war, carrying dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.

title: The winter lines
body: Through the first winter of the war the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the quarter of the harbour below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.

title: Grain from Seann Warr
body: The farming town of Seann Warr in the south-east, not the salt port of the same name in the west, sends grain to the hills through the winter by the eastern roads. The council's roll lists the carts.

title: Hunger in the capital
body: Cathair dhearg goes short through the winter, its harbour held by the Residency. The custodians share out the grain by household. The roll records that the custodians took the same share as everyone else.

title: The burning of the third currency's records
body: Rebels destroy the human administration's tithe ledgers in three separate raids — an act later chroniclers treat as symbolically decisive even though its practical effect was small.

title: The counting-house at Ros dhomhain
body: The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, inside the lines. Men of the harbour quarter led by Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.

title: The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh
body: The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the portion owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and were refused by their own people.

title: The weigh-house at Muileann chrom
body: The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers. The ore of the hills since the first contract had been entered there by the ton. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.

title: The fight at Cnoc ghorm
body: Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to recover the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the last attempt of the war by the Administration to reach the mining district.

title: The harbour quarter changes sides
body: The Ròdaich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter, after the counting-house raid, open the lower gates to the council's companies. Strake is left holding the Residency and the Company's quays alone.

title: Cuan uaine opens its harbour
body: The harbour of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, opens to the council's boats. With it and the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter both lost, the Residency can be supplied only by sea.

title: Strake abandons the Residency
body: Lionel Strake evacuates the Residency by sea with his officials, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and removes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of everything but its furniture.

title: Ros bheag the last seat
body: At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what remains of the Administration. The human families of the west and the south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.

title: Outposts at Ros àrsaidh
body: Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.

title: Hunger in Ros bheag
body: With the roads cut and no ships from the west, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. The Company's stores are opened to the human families and to the Ròdaich townsfolk alike, on Strake's order, the one act of his that the Ròdaich record credits.

title: Cuan shean refuses the humans
body: The custodians of Cuan shean, the town where the first humans came ashore, close its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll notes the irony without comment.

title: The families of Baile dhìreach
body: At Baile dhìreach the descendants of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, are asked by each side which they are. The record says most of them refused to answer, and that neither side forced them.

title: The last ship from the west
body: The last ship recorded arriving from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and she sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.

title: The truce of Àth àrsaidh
body: Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession. They agree a truce: the humans remaining on Rodos to withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, the council to leave the concession towns standing.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns
body: Baile Mòr ruadh, the largest town of the north-west, is named in the truce as the place where the columns will be received. Its Ròdaich people are given the choice of staying or going south. The record gives the numbers of each and they are close.

title: The columns go north
body: The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and that none was helped.

title: The columns at Àth chrom
body: The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on the way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and the count is the last the Ròdaich make of the humans on Rodos in this age.

title: Àth leathan
body: At Àth leathan, on the last stage before the northern territory, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town record that the humans asked the name of the place, and that the name was written down by several of them.

title: The ship that sailed west
body: Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails west from Cuan shean with his officials in the last ship on the island that could make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom records her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Rodos records her arriving anywhere.

title: The beacons relit
body: The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, continue to be kept, with nothing in them.

title: The rolls sent to Muileann chaol
body: The custodians send what survives of the age's rolls, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.

title: The Severance
body: The war ends with the crossing itself closed. Whatever let humans reach Rodos shuts. The humans still on the island are shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in its immediate wake.

title: The Tuathaich homeland fixed
body: Human descendants stranded by the Severance are formally settled in the island's north — a confinement, not a homecoming, though later generations will simply call it home.

title: The Severance companies stood down
body: The war-companies that fought the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls are handed to the council rather than burned, and the companies are never formally abolished; they survive as names on a list.

title: The boundary stones set
body: Stones are set on the roads running north to mark where the Tuathaich territory begins. No wall follows them. Many still stand at the roadside, and nobody has been paid to move them.

title: The hungry year at Doire ghlas
body: Cut off from the stores that used to come over the water from an Tìr Thall, the northern settlements go short of grain in their first year alone. Tuathaich memory, taken down long afterwards, puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. No Ròdaich count was made.

title: The human counting-houses emptied
body: Council clerks enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off everything written. What the raids of the war left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, because few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.

title: The north-west ports without a master
body: At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh, the humans' harbour officers leave with the last ships before the crossing closes, taking their keys. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks on the harbour stores and share out what they find by household.

title: Rìoghachd Ròdais declared
body: The state formally restyles itself a kingdom in form, whatever it remains in function — the same contradiction its own records still carry today.

title: The Moot at Caol mhòr
body: Tuathaich householders from the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose a speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Ròdaich law. It meets anyway and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from this meeting to the present.

title: The council of the kingdom seated
body: A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest continuous record of the state in this age.

title: The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over
body: The customs sheds the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the kingdom's largest port, pass to Ròdaich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff in force for want of another and translates it line by line over the following years.

title: The ship sent west
body: The council sends a ship out past the western capes to look for the crossing the humans used. It comes back after a month of open water and reports nothing: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent.

title: Niall crowned
body: The first ruler of the restored kingdom takes the throne at Cathair dhearg — the opening name in the line the state's own chronicles keep unbroken from here forward.

title: A saying enters speech
body: The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-over of power. Its first written use is in a Cathair dhearg tavern ledger, set against a debt settled without argument.

title: The shires drawn
body: The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only complete ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and does not say so.

title: The maoir appointed
body: A maor is appointed to each shire to collect the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Ròdaich, lodged in the seat towns; at Ceann mhòr the maor's house is the old human magistrate's, and the townspeople call it by the old name.

title: The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr
body: The first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, Coinneach mac Ailein, holds his court under the market roof of the town, since the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps the court there after the new courthouse is built, and so do his successors.

title: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
body: The Great Wave strikes the southern coast without warning, devastating Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night — the first disaster the new state responds to on its own terms.

title: The dead of the Great Wave counted
body: Relief parties from Cathair dhearg reach Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over nine hundred. The harbour at Cuan dhearg is gone. Its boats are found in the fields behind the town.

title: Achadh mhin under salt
body: The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury, the first relief the restored kingdom ever grants.

title: Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill
body: Cnoc chaol is rebuilt on the slope behind the old town, out of the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townspeople call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.

title: Tonn
body: The accounts gathered from survivors by the relief parties use 'tonn', wave, for anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.

title: The wave's reach on Eilean mhin
body: The Great Wave also crosses the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where no one then lived year-round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.

title: The old human coinage withdrawn
body: Every remaining piece of human currency is formally demonetized. A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with obsidian-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year.

title: The mint at Cathair dhearg
body: A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from obsidian dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.

title: The northern savings voided
body: Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. With its withdrawal those savings are worth their metal by weight and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.

title: Joseph Marlow's ploughshares
body: At Doire mhin in the north a smith named Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, which he sells back to them at the cost of the charcoal. Tuathaich songs still name him.

title: The coin at Inis thais
body: At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is short for most of the year and the town's merchants trade in chits written on the Wolf house's paper. The chits are redeemed at the Wolf house door when the coin arrives, and the house keeps a tenth.

title: Creideamh nan Ròdach formalized
body: The Obsidian Rite becomes organized doctrine rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched.

title: The first high custodian of the Rite
body: Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Creideamh nan Ròdach and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the Rite's largest house stands. His first charge is a written order of worship. There had never been one.

title: The Hawk houses refuse
body: The houses of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig around Cnoc bheag decline the new order of worship, holding that the Rite's older form needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. The long quarrel between the two forms of the Rite begins here.

title: The Wolf houses stand aside
body: The houses of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh in the south-west, whose god Clach is not the Rite's, are asked to send witnesses to the formalizing of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter saying they wish it well.

title: The Moot's schoolhouse petition
body: Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Ròdais and that it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.

title: The capital's faith and the court
body: The house of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, as it had been before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks for a share of the keeping and is refused.

title: The first post-Severance census
body: The state counts its own population for the first time since reclaiming the island — and quietly notes, without further comment, exactly how few obsidian-touched individuals actually exist.

title: The count taken from the road
body: Ròdaich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road, without entering most houses. The Moot keeps its own tally the same year. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side keeps its own.

title: The circuit justices
body: Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, the first of them Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit covers eleven shires of the south-west and takes most of a year to ride once.

title: Muileann bhàn's waterworks
body: Muileann bhàn, on the southern plain, builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn how it was done.

title: The Leòid ruling
body: Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, while the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age that follows.

title: The ore line repaired
body: The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places during the Severance war, is repaired as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.

title: The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated
body: The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt under the humans, is re-dedicated with a Ròdais name-stone. The humans' stone is not removed. It is turned to face the river.

title: The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach
body: The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, since the vines have broken too many stones to find room. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.

title: Creideamh nan Tuathach persists
body: Tuathaich communities keep their own folk-shamanic tradition alive in the north — including, quietly, the First Canoe fragment the Ròdaich priesthood still calls superstition.

title: The Grey Night kept openly
body: At Baile chrom in the far north-west, the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the rites of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open for the first time since the Severance. The cult keeps one night of silence in the year for Sìne, the Peaceful Goose. Outsiders are not told which night it is.

title: The Scorpion houses of the north
body: Most Tuathaich towns keep the worship of Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion, as the Ròdaich of the west coast do; how the settlers came to it the record does not say. A house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe is built at Cnoc ghorm, the largest in the north.

title: The school of the Scorpion at Cnoc ghorm
body: The Scorpion house at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests, teaching in the humans' tongue and reading the Scorpion's scripture in the Ròdais text the west-coast houses use. It is the only place in the north where both are taught.

title: The border wall proposed
body: A formal boundary between Ròdaich and Tuathaich territory is proposed for the first time. It is rejected — not out of principle, records suggest, but because it's considered unnecessary. The two populations are already staying apart on their own.

title: The minute on the wall
body: The council minute that rejects the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' It is initialled by five of the twelve councillors, and the other seven did not sign against it.

title: The Allt an Àigh walk
body: Followers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach keep up their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water the old tales say brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite discourage the walk and do not forbid it.

title: The walkers at Achadh gharbh
body: The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, which by the end of the decade holds names from fifty shires.

title: Extraction resumes at full scale
body: The mine's post-Severance yield matches, then exceeds, its colonial-era output. Nothing about the method changed. Only who profits did.

title: The Sloc Mòr concession
body: The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The terms give the Crown a fifth of the yield. They are the humans' terms with the names changed.

title: The night-shift kept
body: The council declines to end the continuous working of the vein, day and night, that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest and then bless the shafts.

title: The pit towns fill
body: Ròdaich families from the hungry east move to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years, and its hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and enlarged twice in the same span.

title: Baile thais grows on the ore road
body: Baile thais, where the ore road from the central mountains meets the east coast, takes on carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its population doubles in a decade, and the town is given a shire court.

title: Raiders off Cathair gheal
body: Ships that no longer fly any flag, some crewed by men who once served the human administration, begin raiding the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first and are not defended.

title: The ore line reaches the Sloc Mòr
body: The repaired railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first ore train from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg runs under the kingdom's name and on the humans' rails.

title: The quarry at Achadh dhomhain
body: The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a black-veined grey stone, is cut and sold as building stone under the house of Mac Ùisdein's quarry-mark. It is used for public buildings across the south for the next forty years.

title: The shunting yards at Muileann chrom
body: The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where ore trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The yard's families, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted separately by the Board and live apart in rows by the lines.

title: The guild system restored
body: The old apprentice-binding custom from the Holy Age is revived in modified form, now explicitly reserved for Ròdaich applicants only.

title: The Guild of Hewers chartered
body: The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is taken with a hand on a piece of ore. Its rolls are open to Ròdaich only, as the charter requires.

title: The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain
body: The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.

title: The indentures broken
body: At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral, Tuathaich boys already bound to Ròdaich masters are released from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labour, outside the guilds and their wages.

title: The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh
body: The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the southern coast east of the capital, take a guild charter and a monopoly of supplying the Crown's patrol boats. The monopoly outlasts the patrol boats.

title: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin
body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the ore lamps used in every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp and is the only guild mark the humans' traders had ever copied.

title: The weavers of Baile chiar
body: The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth, woven from southern wool, undersells the northern cloth at the fair until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.

title: Agnes Pike's school
body: Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with Moot money and without the council's leave. Within a decade there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never closes them.

title: The Cill ghlas district reopened
body: The mining district closed since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. The first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line, on the surveyors' word.

title: The Leòid circuit in the north
body: Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. She finds for the Crown in fifteen, citing her own ruling.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies
body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound as a single book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.

title: Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
body: A great library is established at Muileann chaol — the institution that will eventually keep the most complete surviving record of everything in this chronicle.

title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper
body: Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is appointed the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what survived of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.

title: A chur san Leabharlann
body: Within a few years, 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything made settled and beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is recorded as disliking the phrase, on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it.

title: The first readers
body: The library's first reading room opens to anyone who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader entered in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, asking for the humans' plans of their hulls.

title: The bath-house at the hot springs
body: A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year lists four hundred men by name and shift.

title: The keepers of the five lights
body: The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Ròdaich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the keeper is a Ròdaich man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant tells him to report what he sees on land as well as at sea.

title: The Muileann chaol town grows
body: Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle in Muileann chaol around the library. The town takes a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.

title: The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach
body: A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For the next half-century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.

title: The first royal chronicler appointed
body: A formal office is created specifically to maintain the kingdom's records — the direct ancestor of the archive this very document draws from.

title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill
body: The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol, not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.

title: The first chronicle circuit
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one; few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.

title: The chest from Inis bheag
body: The chronicle clerks at Inis bheag on the north-east coast are shown a parish book going back before the humans' coming, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied and not taken.

title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag
body: A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.

title: The thing off the north-west cape
body: Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh report a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill records the report and adds that the same waters are where the raiders shelter.

title: The Eilean dhubh sheep-count
body: A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks on Eilean dhubh, the largest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.

title: Cathair gheal arms its boats
body: The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders out of the bay. The council, asked for help twice, had sent none. It later fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.

title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr
body: A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr, paid for by the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and ore markets are moved to its foot.

title: The Wolf house at Caol leathan
body: The Wolf house at Caol leathan, the largest of the faith, is rebuilt with a tower from which a bell rings at the hours. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.

title: Fèill Muileann òg established
body: An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering, drawing trade from every province the state controls.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules
body: The first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, Oighrig nic Mhathain, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods sold only through Ròdaich factors. The rules are read aloud at each fair's opening to this day.

title: The fair's road
body: The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the fair's carts, passing Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it.

title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll
body: The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townspeople call it the fair's wall, and the fair's carters call it something else.

title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
body: His daughter succeeds him without contest — mortal succession within an immortal-adjacent aristocracy, unremarkable at the time, unusual in hindsight.

title: The chronicler's use of the saying
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall', the first time the saying appears in the royal record. It is the only idiom she allows into the chronicle in her whole tenure.

title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn
body: The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where the ancestors of forty families are named aloud each year by their living heads. The list is copied to the library the next year and grows by a few names every year after.

title: Cuan ruadh's harbour light
body: Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has no lighthouse of the five, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole, lit with ore bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board declines to take it on.

title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan established
body: A brutal annual melee tournament begins at Ceann leathan, ostensibly a martial tradition, increasingly a release valve for a population with fewer and fewer other outlets.

title: Calum Ruadh
body: The first champion of the Còmhrag the record remembers is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer from Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to carry arms in any shire.

title: Ceann leathan's inns
body: Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the Còmhrag crowds. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.

title: The ore-ships of Ros gheal
body: Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of the dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.

title: Splatter and Dodge's generation born
body: A cluster of births in the Class-08-adjacent shunting families — the generation that will grow up to become Dubhan's closest allies, Seachran and Brean among them.

title: Seann Bhral in the south
body: Seann Bhral on the south coast, not to be confused with its namesake in the west, becomes the kingdom's largest fishing port, landing more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.

title: The circus at Seann Chwen
body: The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what the acts were meant to show. Neither, the clerk adds, could the crowd, which came back the next night.

title: The Scorpion at Seann Bhral
body: The house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, refuses to admit Tuathaich worshippers from the north who come for its feast. Its keeper says the god is the same and the house is not.

title: The northern Scorpion feast
body: Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich worshippers of the Scorpion hold the feast at Cnoc ghorm instead. It is kept there every year after, and the northern feast is larger than the western within a generation.

title: The Depletion first acknowledged
body: Survey reports begin quietly noting the vein's declining yield. The state does not act on them for years.

title: Iain Mapa's survey
body: The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measurements of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to the east and south. The Board files the survey without circulating it, and Iain Mapa is moved to the silver works at Muileann chiar.

title: The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr
body: The Mine Board, which had sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. Its surveys are kept there, not sent to the library, by the Board's own rule.

title: The Grey Night forbidden
body: A Ròdaich magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night cult as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil moves indoors and goes on.

title: The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened
body: The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is reopened with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.

title: Achadh mhin resettled
body: The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old boundaries from the humans' survey.

title: Eòghan crowned
body: Brìghde's reign ends young — no cause is recorded publicly. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne amid the first real succession tension the restored kingdom has faced.

title: The succession entry
body: The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the fact and nothing more. The chroniclers who followed Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.

title: Dissent recorded in council
body: For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.

title: Inis bhàn's fire
body: Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the north-central coast and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.

title: Dubhan born
body: Born mortal, into the exact confinement the Severance created, decades after the war that closed the island to the people his line descends from.

title: The Tuathaich schools counted
body: The Moot counts eleven schools in the north teaching in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is among the three.

title: The stone house of Mac Ùisdein
body: Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the largest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.

title: The northern fishing grounds
body: Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are reserved to Ròdaich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, which the raiders also work.

title: Doire shean's harbour
body: Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Wolf country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The Wolf house lends the money and takes the harbour dues.

title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin
body: Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Ròdaich building and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar orders the finds catalogued as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.

title: Làrach an Teampaill measured
body: The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east but do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.

title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
body: A scribe of the library copies the inscription on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It matches no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk is fenced.
